great.name: Château Margaux
great.what: First Growth of the Margaux appellation: mostly Cabernet Sauvignon from gravel soils, aged in new French oak.
great.why: The most perfumed and silky of the Médoc's First Growths: violets, cassis and cedar with a velvet texture. Lovers call it the iron fist in a velvet glove.

great.name: Château Mouton Rothschild
great.what: Pauillac First Growth (promoted in 1973), around 80% Cabernet Sauvignon.
great.why: Opulent blackcurrant, cedar and coffee, and a new label by a famous artist every year: Picasso, Warhol, Bacon. A collector's wine as much as a drinker's.

great.name: Pétrus
great.what: A tiny Pomerol estate of pure Merlot on a buttonhole of blue clay.
great.why: Merlot at its most profound: plum, truffle and chocolate with a creamy, endless texture. Scarce and outside any classification, it is one of the world's most expensive wines.

great.name: Château Cheval Blanc
great.what: Saint-Émilion's great estate, unusual for its high share of Cabernet Franc on gravel and clay.
great.why: Floral, spicy and silky, fresh even when young. The 1947, a legend, appears in the film Ratatouille.

great.name: Château d'Yquem
great.what: The only Premier Cru Supérieur of 1855: botrytized Sémillon picked berry by berry, sometimes over many passes.
great.why: Apricot, honey, saffron and crème brûlée with fresh acidity; it lives for a century. In poor years none is made.

great.name: Château Lafite Rothschild
great.what: First Growth of Pauillac on deep gravel, mostly Cabernet Sauvignon.
great.why: The most elegant of the Médoc giants: cedar, cassis and lead pencil with a silky finish.

great.name: Château Latour
great.what: First Growth beside the Gironde, around 80% Cabernet from the walled Enclos.
great.why: Power and consistency: dense, iron-fisted wine that shines even in difficult years.

great.name: Château Haut-Brion
great.what: The only First Growth outside the Médoc, now in Bordeaux's suburbs.
great.why: Smoky, earthy, tobacco-scented; sold by name in London since the 1660s.

great.name: Château Ausone
great.what: A tiny estate on Saint-Émilion's limestone slope, named after the Roman poet Ausonius.
great.why: Mineral, floral Cabernet Franc built to live for half a century.

great.name: Le Pin
great.what: A garage-sized Pomerol cellar founded in 1979, pure Merlot.
great.why: Lush, exotic and seductive; it started the 'garage wine' craze.

great.name: Château Léoville Las Cases
great.what: Second Growth whose vineyard touches Latour.
great.why: Built like a First Growth for a fraction of the price: tight, classic, very long-lived.

great.name: Château Ducru-Beaucaillou
great.what: Second Growth on 'beautiful pebbles' facing the estuary.
great.why: Polished, harmonious Saint-Julien with fine-grained tannins.

great.name: Château Pichon Longueville Comtesse de Lalande
great.what: Second Growth with more Merlot than most of Pauillac.
great.why: Opulent and charming: the seductive side of Pauillac.

great.name: Château Palmer
great.what: Third Growth, farmed biodynamically, with an unusually high share of Merlot.
great.why: Silky, perfumed and plush; often rivals the First Growths.

great.name: Château Cos d'Estournel
great.what: Second Growth with a chai topped by Indian pagodas.
great.why: Exotic spice and power, the most flamboyant Saint-Estèphe.

great.name: Château Montrose
great.what: Second Growth on gravel overlooking the Gironde.
great.why: Dense and structured, a wine to buy for your grandchildren.

great.name: Château Lynch-Bages
great.what: Fifth Growth that drinks like a Second.
great.why: Generous cassis, mint and cedar; a crowd favorite in restaurants worldwide.

great.name: Château Pontet-Canet
great.what: Fifth Growth worked biodynamically, partly by horse.
great.why: Pure, vibrant fruit; one of Bordeaux's great success stories of the 2000s.

great.name: Château Figeac
great.what: Saint-Émilion estate on gravel, with lots of Cabernet; top rank since 2022.
great.why: Fresh, aromatic and elegant, unlike the plush Merlot of its neighbors.

great.name: Château Angélus
great.what: The estate with a bell on its label, at the foot of Saint-Émilion's slope.
great.why: Rich, modern and opulent; a star in the 2000s.

great.name: Château La Mission Haut-Brion
great.why: Darker and more powerful than Haut-Brion, with smoky gravel character.

great.name: Château Smith Haut Lafitte Blanc
great.what: One of the great dry whites of Bordeaux, barrel-fermented Sauvignon.
great.why: Citrus, toast and minerality that ages beautifully.

great.name: Château Climens
great.what: Barsac First Growth, pure Sémillon on limestone.
great.why: The freshest of the great sweet wines: lemon, honey and white flowers.

great.name: Château Calon-Ségur
great.what: Third Growth with a heart on its label.
great.why: Classic, savory claret; a Valentine's Day favorite.

great.name: Château Sociando-Mallet
great.what: Unclassified Haut-Médoc estate that ages like a classed growth.
great.why: Serious Bordeaux at an everyday-luxury price.

great.name: Romanée-Conti
great.what: A 1.8-hectare Grand Cru in Vosne-Romanée, owned whole by the Domaine; only about 5,000–6,000 bottles a year.
great.why: Pinot Noir's most famous vineyard: rose, spice and red fruit, weightless yet intense. Rarity makes it the most expensive wine at release.

great.name: Chablis Grand Cru Les Clos
great.what: The biggest and grandest of Chablis' seven Grand Cru plots, on fossil-rich Kimmeridgian limestone.
great.why: Chardonnay as pure as it gets: lemon, oyster shell and flint, ageing into honey and hazelnut. Great value next to Côte d'Or whites.

great.name: La Tâche
great.what: A Vosne-Romanée Grand Cru owned entirely by the Domaine.
great.why: Spicy, exotic and dense: for many, the most complete of the DRC wines.

great.name: Musigny
great.what: The largest owner of Chambolle's greatest Grand Cru.
great.why: Lace and velvet: Pinot Noir at its most perfumed and silky.

great.name: Chambertin
great.what: Napoleon's favorite vineyard, from Gevrey's most revered grower.
great.why: Power with grace; a benchmark for Grand Cru Burgundy.

great.name: Gevrey-Chambertin Clos Saint-Jacques
great.what: A Premier Cru so good it sells for Grand Cru prices.
great.why: Red fruit, spice and earth, refined and long.

great.name: Clos de la Roche
great.what: Grand Cru in Morey-Saint-Denis, fermented with whole bunches.
great.why: Floral, spicy and silky with a stony backbone.

great.name: Bonnes-Mares
great.what: Grand Cru straddling Chambolle and Morey from a cult grower.
great.why: Muscular yet silky, among the most sought-after Burgundies.

great.name: Clos de Vougeot
great.what: The monks' walled vineyard, from Henri Jayer's heirs in spirit.
great.why: Dark fruit and spice from the upper, best part of the Clos.

great.name: Vosne-Romanée
great.what: Village wine from Burgundy's most famous commune.
great.why: A first taste of Vosne's spice and silk without Grand Cru prices.

great.name: Nuits-Saint-Georges Les Saint-Georges
great.what: The best Premier Cru of Nuits, long proposed for Grand Cru.

great.name: Volnay Clos des Ducs
great.what: A walled Premier Cru monopole from a pioneer of domaine bottling.
great.why: The most delicate, floral side of red Burgundy.

great.name: Pommard Les Rugiens
great.what: Pommard's top Premier Cru on iron-rich red soil.

great.name: Beaune Clos des Mouches
great.what: A Premier Cru the négociant house Drouhin has owned since 1921.

great.name: Corton-Charlemagne
great.what: Grand Cru white said to have been Charlemagne's vineyard.
great.why: Steely, powerful Chardonnay that needs years to open.

great.name: Bâtard-Montrachet
great.what: Grand Cru next to Le Montrachet, from Puligny's most famous domaine.
great.why: Rich, honeyed and mineral, the essence of great white Burgundy.

great.name: Puligny-Montrachet
great.what: Village Puligny from a biodynamic pioneer.
great.why: Floral, precise and mineral white Burgundy.

great.name: Meursault
great.what: Meursault from a grower famous for tension rather than butter.
great.why: Lemony, nutty and electric; a cult favorite.

great.name: Chassagne-Montrachet
great.what: Chassagne from a family that defined the village.
great.why: Generous, hazelnut-scented Chardonnay with fresh acidity.

great.name: Chablis Premier Cru Montée de Tonnerre
great.what: Chablis' cult domaine, aged in old barrels.
great.why: Oyster shell, lemon and saline depth that last for decades.

great.name: Chablis
great.what: Village Chablis from the region's biggest Grand Cru owner.
great.why: Crisp, mineral, unoaked Chardonnay: the classic oyster wine.

great.name: Pouilly-Fuissé Tête de Cru
great.what: The Mâconnais' top appellation, from its historic estate.
great.why: Ripe, round Chardonnay with real Burgundian class.

great.name: Morgon
great.what: Gamay from a father of the natural-wine movement.
great.why: Juicy, joyful red fruit with real depth; Beaujolais at its best.

great.name: Moulin-à-Vent
great.what: The most structured Beaujolais cru, named after its windmill.

great.name: Échezeaux
great.what: The 'entry' Grand Cru of the world's most famous domaine.
great.why: A glimpse of DRC's magic: rose, spice and silk.

great.name: Dom Pérignon
great.what: Moët & Chandon's prestige cuvée, only ever vintage, roughly half Chardonnay and half Pinot Noir, aged seven years or more.
great.why: Smoky, toasty and creamy with fine bubbles; the most famous Champagne name in the world, and it ages beautifully.

great.name: Krug Grande Cuvée
vintages: Each edition blends 100+ wines from 10+ years
great.what: A multi-vintage Champagne fermented in small old oak barrels and blended from a huge library of reserve wines.
great.why: Rich, nutty, brioche and citrus with great depth: Champagne with the weight of fine white Burgundy. Each bottle carries an 'ID' to look up its blend.

great.name: Krug Clos du Mesnil
great.what: A single walled Chardonnay vineyard in Le Mesnil-sur-Oger.
great.why: Pure, intense Blanc de Blancs of extraordinary length.

great.name: Cristal
great.what: Created for the Russian Tsar in 1876, in a clear bottle.
great.why: Silky, precise and luminous; a symbol of luxury.

great.name: La Grande Année
great.what: Bollinger's vintage cuvée, fermented in barrels.
great.why: Rich, toasty, Pinot-led Champagne; James Bond's choice.

great.name: Special Cuvée
great.what: The house's non-vintage blend, with old reserve wines.
great.why: Full, nutty and generous for a non-vintage.

great.name: Cuvée Sir Winston Churchill
great.what: Named for the house's most famous fan.
great.why: Powerful and structured, made to age.

great.name: Brut Réserve
great.what: A classic non-vintage from a family house in Épernay.

great.name: Salon Le Mesnil
great.what: One wine, one grape, one village, made only in great years.
great.why: Rare, laser-sharp Blanc de Blancs that needs decades.

great.name: Comtes de Champagne Blanc de Blancs
Brut Rosé
great.what: A family house's benchmark pink Champagne.
great.why: Delicate strawberries and finesse; the rosé sommeliers love.

great.name: Yellow Label Brut
great.what: The widow Clicquot's house, famous for its orange-yellow label.

great.name: La Grande Dame
great.what: Clicquot's prestige cuvée, named after the widow herself.

great.name: Blanc de Blancs
great.what: From the oldest Champagne house, founded 1729.
great.why: Bright, creamy Chardonnay in a clear bottle.

great.name: Impérial Brut
great.why: Fresh apple and brioche; the bottle at most celebrations.

great.name: Grand Siècle
great.what: A blend of three great vintages in one cuvée.

great.name: Cuvée Rosé
great.what: Rosé made by skin contact, not blending.
great.why: Vivid red fruit; a pioneer of rosé Champagne.

great.name: Brut Réserve
great.why: Rich, toasty depth far above its price.

great.name: Cuvée 7xx
great.what: A numbered 'non-vintage' that shows one harvest plus reserves.

great.name: Brut Tradition Grand Cru
great.what: Grower Champagne from Ambonnay's Pinot Noir.
great.why: Powerful, vinous Champagne from a cult grower.

great.name: Initial
great.what: Blanc de Blancs from Avize, fermented in barrel.
great.why: The grower who changed Champagne: oxidative, nutty, wine-like.

great.name: Cuis 1er Cru Blanc de Blancs
great.what: Grower Chardonnay from the Côte des Blancs.
great.why: Crisp, chalky value from a respected family.

great.name: Clos des Goisses
great.what: A single, very steep south-facing vineyard above the Marne.
great.why: Ripe, powerful and long-lived, one of Champagne's first single-vineyard wines.

great.name: Grande Réserve
great.why: Vinous, crisp Champagne made without malolactic.

great.name: Belle Époque
great.what: Prestige cuvée in an Art Nouveau anemone bottle.
great.why: Floral, delicate and beautiful on the table.

great.name: Château de Beaucastel
great.what: One of the few Châteauneuf estates to use all 13 permitted grapes, with an unusually high share of Mourvèdre.
great.why: Garrigue herbs, leather and dark berries; it ages for decades. Organic since the 1950s.

great.name: Hermitage La Chapelle
great.what: Syrah from the granite hill of Hermitage, named after the little chapel at its top.
great.why: Black olive, violet, smoked meat and pepper: the benchmark of northern Rhône Syrah. The 1961 is one of the wines of the century.

great.name: Côte-Rôtie La Mouline
great.what: One of Guigal's three single-vineyard 'La La' wines.
great.why: Silky Syrah lifted by Viognier: violets and bacon fat.

great.name: Côte-Rôtie La Landonne
great.what: Pure Syrah from a steep, iron-rich slope.
great.why: The darkest, most powerful of the 'La Las'.

great.name: Côte-Rôtie Brune et Blonde
great.what: Guigal's classic blend from the 'brown' and 'blond' slopes.
great.why: The easiest way into Côte-Rôtie's perfume.

great.name: Hermitage
great.what: A blend of plots across the hill from a family there since 1481.
great.why: Profound, complete Syrah: the hill's reference.

great.name: Hermitage Monier de la Sizeranne
great.what: Hermitage from a biodynamic house, with a Braille label.

great.name: Château Rayas
great.what: Pure Grenache from sandy soils in a forest clearing.

great.name: La Crau
great.what: From the stony La Crau plateau.
great.why: Garrigue, kirsch and stones: classic Châteauneuf.

great.name: Châteauneuf-du-Pape
great.what: A family estate with plots across the appellation.
great.why: Elegant, age-worthy and Wine Spectator's 2007 wine of the year.

great.name: Châteauneuf-du-Pape
great.what: One of the oldest estates in Châteauneuf.

great.name: Châteauneuf-du-Pape Vieilles Vignes
great.what: Old-vine Grenache from a family domaine.

great.name: Réserve des Célestins
great.what: From a tiny, legendary cellar, released only in great years.
great.why: Deep, layered Grenache from a vanished era.

great.name: Cornas
great.what: The reference for Cornas, made traditionally.
great.why: Wild, savory Syrah that rewards patience.

great.name: Cornas Reynard
great.what: Tiny production from steep granite terraces.

great.name: Côte-Rôtie
great.what: A blend of many parcels across the slope.

great.name: Condrieu Coteau de Vernon
great.what: Viognier from the family who saved Condrieu in the 1960s.

great.name: Château-Grillet
great.what: A one-estate appellation, one of the smallest in France.
great.why: Rare, textured Viognier in a historic amphitheater.

great.name: Saint-Joseph
great.why: Pure, peppery Syrah, a bargain for northern Rhône lovers.

great.name: Crozes-Hermitage
great.what: Crozes from the grower who lifted the appellation.

great.name: Gigondas
great.what: Grenache from slopes below the Dentelles de Montmirail.
great.why: Châteauneuf's character at a friendlier price.

great.name: Gigondas
great.what: From a Roman-era estate with a cellar carved in rock.

great.name: Vacqueyras
great.what: Biodynamic Vacqueyras with a different name every year.

great.name: Tavel
great.what: From France's only appellation for rosé alone.

great.name: Côtes du Rhône
great.what: Among the most widely sold quality reds in the world.

great.name: Silex
great.what: Pouilly-Fumé from flint soils by the late rebel winemaker.
great.why: Sauvignon Blanc as great white wine: smoke, citrus and depth.

great.name: Sancerre La Côte des Monts Damnés
great.what: From Sancerre's most famous steep slope.

great.name: Sancerre
great.what: Biodynamic family estate in Sancerre town.

great.name: Pouilly-Fumé
great.what: From the Château du Nozet, the appellation's flagship.

great.name: Vouvray Le Haut-Lieu Sec
great.what: Biodynamic Chenin from Vouvray's reference estate.
great.why: Quince, honey and acidity that lasts decades.

great.name: Vouvray Clos du Bourg Moelleux
great.what: Sweet Chenin from a historic walled vineyard.
great.why: Honey and apple with endless freshness.

great.name: Quarts de Chaume
great.what: A Grand Cru for sweet Chenin in the Layon.

great.name: Clos de la Coulée de Serrant
great.what: A one-estate appellation from a father of biodynamics.
great.why: Powerful, waxy Chenin unlike anything else.

great.name: Saumur-Champigny Le Bourg
great.what: The cult Cabernet Franc of the Loire.
great.why: Silky, deep and sought after worldwide.

great.name: Chinon Clos de la Dioterie
great.what: Old vines on clay-limestone in Chinon.

great.name: Chinon Les Grézeaux
great.what: From a family that defined modern Chinon.

great.name: Bourgueil Mi-Pente
great.what: Jacky Blot's Bourgueil from a south-facing slope.

great.name: Montlouis Clos du Breuil
great.what: Biodynamic Chenin from Montlouis, across the river from Vouvray.

great.name: Montlouis Rémus
great.producer: Domaine de la Taille aux Loups

great.name: Muscadet Sèvre et Maine Sur Lie
Muscadet L d'Or
great.what: A long-aged Muscadet from a historic family.
great.why: Shows how well Muscadet can age.

great.name: Crémant de Loire Brut

great.why: Champagne-style bubbles at a fraction of the price.

great.name: Sancerre Florès
great.what: Sancerre from Bué, a top village.

great.name: Saumur-Champigny Terres Chaudes
great.what: Biodynamic Cabernet Franc from a single plot.

great.name: Coteaux du Loir L'Effraie
great.what: Chenin from the cool northern Loir valley.

great.name: Barolo Riserva Monfortino
great.what: Nebbiolo from the Cascina Francia vineyard in Serralunga, aged about seven years in huge old casks; only in great years.
great.why: Rose, tar, cherry and iron, with tannins that need decades. The most revered traditional Barolo.

great.name: Barolo Francia
great.what: From the Cascina Francia vineyard in Serralunga, in years without Monfortino.
great.why: Classic, powerful Barolo built to age.

great.name: Barolo
great.what: A traditional blend of crus, aged in big casks.
great.why: Rose, tar and cherry: the soul of old-school Barolo.

great.name: Barbaresco
great.what: The house that put Barbaresco on the world map.

great.name: Sorì San Lorenzo
great.what: A single vineyard that made Angelo Gaja's name.

great.name: Barbaresco Asili
great.what: From the late master of Barbaresco.

great.name: Barbaresco

great.why: Classic Barbaresco at a fair price.

great.name: Barbaresco Riserva Rabajà

great.name: Tignanello
great.what: Antinori's Sangiovese blended with Cabernet and aged in French barriques: a founding Super Tuscan (1971).
great.why: Cherry, spice and vanilla with polished tannins; a modern Tuscan classic that is easier to find than most icons.

great.what: From a high, cool medieval village.

facts: Champagne bottles hold about three times the pressure of a car tire, which is why the cork is wired down.
A 'Jeroboam' is a 3-litre bottle in Champagne and Burgundy, but in Bordeaux the name has meant 4.5 or 5 litres.
Chardonnay is a child of Pinot Noir and Gouais Blanc, a peasant grape medieval nobles tried to ban.
Cabernet Sauvignon was born in 17th-century Bordeaux from a chance crossing of Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc.
The oldest known winery, about 6,100 years old, was found in the Areni-1 cave in Armenia.
Grapes for ice wine are picked frozen on the vine, often at night, at −8 °C or colder.
Phylloxera, a tiny American aphid, destroyed most of Europe's vineyards in the late 1800s.
Almost every European vine today grows on American rootstock, grafted to resist phylloxera.
Chile was never hit by phylloxera, so many of its vines still grow on their own roots.
Carmenère was thought extinct after phylloxera until it was found in Chile in 1994, mistaken for Merlot.
In the 1976 Judgment of Paris, California wines beat top Bordeaux and Burgundy in a blind tasting by French judges.
The 1855 Bordeaux classification was made for a Paris world fair and has changed only twice since.
Château Mouton Rothschild was promoted to First Growth in 1973, the biggest change to the 1855 list.
Each Mouton Rothschild label since 1945 is painted by an artist: Picasso, Miró, Chagall, Warhol and more.
Dom Pérignon did not invent Champagne; he spent his life trying to stop wine from turning fizzy.
Madame Clicquot invented the riddling table around 1816, making clear sparkling wine possible.
Pinot Noir is so old and unstable that it has mutated into Pinot Gris, Pinot Blanc and Pinot Meunier.
Zinfandel and Italy's Primitivo are the same grape, which originally came from Croatia as Tribidrag.
Syrah has nothing to do with the Iranian city of Shiraz; DNA shows it comes from the northern Rhône.
A wine's 'legs' tell you about alcohol and sugar, not quality.
Red wine gets its color from the skins; almost all grape juice, even from black grapes, is clear.
Blanc de Noirs Champagne is a white wine made from black grapes.
Sherry ages under a layer of yeast called flor that protects it from the air.
A solera can mix wine from dozens of vintages; some in Jerez were started over a century ago.
Port is made by adding grape spirit during fermentation, which stops it and keeps the wine sweet.
Madeira is deliberately heated as it ages, a style first discovered on long sea voyages through the tropics.
An opened bottle of Madeira can last for months, because it is already oxidized and heated.
Sauternes owes its honeyed taste to noble rot, a fungus that shrivels grapes and concentrates their sugar.
Tokaji Aszú was being made from botrytized grapes in Hungary before Sauternes was.
The Romans spread vines across Europe, from the Mosel to the Rhône.
The Mosel's steepest vineyard, the Calmont, is about 65° in places: workers use ropes and monorails.
Slate on Mosel slopes stores the day's heat and gives it back to the vines at night.
Riesling can age for decades and often develops a 'petrol' aroma as it gets older.
Grüner Veltliner often smells of white pepper, thanks to the same compound found in peppercorns: rotundone.
Rotundone also gives Syrah its black-pepper note.
Sauvignon Blanc's 'green pepper' smell comes from pyrazines, which fade as the grapes ripen in the sun.
Corked wine smells of wet cardboard because of a compound called TCA, detectable at a few parts per trillion.
About 1–3% of bottles sealed with natural cork are thought to be affected by cork taint.
Most cork comes from Portugal, where cork oaks are stripped about every nine years without being cut down.
New Zealand bottles more than 90% of its wine under screw caps.
A standard bottle holds 750 ml: about five glasses of 150 ml.
A 'Nebuchadnezzar' bottle holds 15 litres, the same as 20 standard bottles.
Wine tastes different from one glass shape to another because the shape steers aromas to your nose.
Your nose does most of the tasting: the tongue only senses sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami.
Tannins come from grape skins, seeds, stems and oak; they make your mouth feel dry.
Acid makes your mouth water; that is how tasters judge acidity.
Most wine is made to be drunk within a few years, not cellared.
Oak barrels can add vanilla, coconut, toast and spice; American oak tends to give more coconut than French oak.
A new French oak barrel can cost well over $1,000, which is why oaked wines often cost more.
Malolactic conversion turns sharp malic acid into softer lactic acid and can give wine a buttery smell.
Sparkling wine made by the traditional method ferments a second time inside the very bottle you buy.
Prosecco gets its bubbles in big steel tanks, which keeps it fresh and fruity.
Champagne must age at least 15 months before release; vintage Champagne at least three years.
Burgundy's vineyards were mapped plot by plot by Cistercian monks in the Middle Ages.
A Burgundy Grand Cru vineyard can be split among dozens of owners: Clos de Vougeot has over 80.
Napoleon's inheritance laws split Burgundy's vineyards into tiny plots shared by many heirs.
Romanée-Conti covers less than two hectares and makes only around 5,000–6,000 bottles a year.
Bordeaux's 'Right Bank' is mostly Merlot; the 'Left Bank' is mostly Cabernet Sauvignon.
Pétrus, on Pomerol's blue clay, has never been part of any official classification.
Saint-Émilion's classification is revised about every ten years, and wines can be demoted.
The Dutch drained the Médoc's marshes in the 1600s, creating some of Bordeaux's greatest vineyards.
Bordeaux was English for 300 years after 1152, which is why the British still call red Bordeaux 'claret'.
Châteauneuf-du-Pape takes its name from the 14th-century popes who lived in nearby Avignon.
Châteauneuf-du-Pape allows 13 grape varieties (18 counting color variants).
The big round stones in some Châteauneuf vineyards, called galets roulés, store heat for the vines.
Beaujolais Nouveau is released on the third Thursday of November, only weeks after harvest.
Carbonic maceration starts fermentation inside whole, uncrushed grapes and gives Beaujolais its candy-like fruit.
Chianti's black rooster logo comes from a medieval legend about a border race between Florence and Siena.
Sassicaia, a Cabernet from the Tuscan coast, began life as a humble table wine and inspired the Super Tuscans.
Nebbiolo is named after nebbia, the autumn fog of Piedmont's Langhe hills.
Barolo must age at least 38 months before release, 18 of them in wood.
Amarone is made from grapes dried for about three months, which concentrates their sugar and flavor.
Italy has more native grape varieties than any other country: well over 500.
Rioja Gran Reserva must age at least five years before release, two of them in oak.
Spain has more land under vine than any other country.
Albariño from Rías Baixas is grown on high pergolas so Atlantic breezes keep the grapes dry.
Port grapes were traditionally trodden by foot in stone tanks called lagares; some still are.
The Douro Valley was one of the first wine regions to be legally demarcated, in 1756.
Vinho Verde means 'green wine' because it is drunk young, not because of its color.
Santorini's vines are woven into low baskets, called kouloura, to shelter grapes from wind and sun.
Some of Santorini's vine roots are said to be centuries old; phylloxera never reached the volcanic island.
Georgia has made wine in clay pots called qvevri, buried in the ground, for about 8,000 years.
Orange wine is white wine made like red: the juice sits on the skins for days or months.
Lebanon's Château Musar kept making wine through 15 years of civil war.
The Temple of Bacchus at Baalbek, in Lebanon's Bekaa Valley, is one of the best-preserved Roman temples.
Château Ksara's cellars in Lebanon run through two kilometres of Roman-era caves.
Malbec came from Cahors in France but became famous in Argentina's high Mendoza vineyards.
Some Argentine vineyards in Salta grow above 3,000 m, among the highest in the world.
High altitude gives cooler nights, so grapes keep their acidity while thick skins build color.
South Africa's Pinotage is a 1925 cross of Pinot Noir and Cinsault, then called Hermitage there.
Vin de Constance from South Africa was a favorite of Napoleon in exile on Saint Helena.
Australia's Barossa Valley has some of the world's oldest Shiraz vines, planted in the 1840s.
Penfolds Grange began as a secret project: the winemaker was told to stop, and kept making it anyway.
Marlborough's first Sauvignon Blanc vines were planted only in 1975; it is now New Zealand's biggest region.
Oregon became famous for Pinot Noir because its climate resembles Burgundy's.
Napa Valley grows only about 4% of California's wine grapes but earns a large share of its value.
Thomas Jefferson tried for decades to grow European vines at Monticello and never succeeded.
Wine needs roughly 30 to 50 degrees of latitude to thrive, in both hemispheres: the 'wine belt'.
Cool regions make lighter wines with more acidity; warm regions make riper, fuller, more alcoholic wines.
A vine usually needs about three years before it gives grapes good enough for wine.
Old vines give fewer grapes, but many growers think their wines taste more concentrated.
Veraison is the moment grapes soften and change color, about 40–50 days before harvest.
Diurnal range, the gap between day and night temperatures, helps grapes keep fresh acidity.
Grape skins hold most of a wine's color, tannin and aroma compounds.
A ton of grapes makes roughly 700 to 750 bottles of wine.
The 100-point scale was popularized by Robert Parker in the 1980s.
On the 100-point scale, a wine really starts at 50: anything 90 or above is 'outstanding'.
Jancis Robinson rates wines out of 20; many European critics prefer the 20-point scale.
Decanting helps a young, tannic red open up and separates an old wine from its sediment.
Sediment in an old red is natural: color and tannin molecules that bonded and fell out over time.
Tartrate crystals, sometimes called 'wine diamonds', are harmless and a sign of a wine not over-processed.
Serving a red too warm makes it taste soupy and alcoholic; a slight chill often helps.
Serving a white too cold mutes its aromas; take a fine white out of the fridge a little before pouring.
Salt in food makes wine taste softer and fruitier, which is why Champagne and fries work so well.
Sweet food makes dry wine taste thin and sour: the wine should be at least as sweet as the dessert.
Chili heat makes high-alcohol wines burn; off-dry Riesling is a classic match for spicy food.
Fatty food softens tannin, which is why steak and Cabernet are such old friends.
Sommelier comes from an old French word for the officer in charge of a royal household's provisions.
The Master Sommelier exam is so hard that fewer than 300 people have passed it.
The Court of Master Sommeliers was founded in England in 1977; the Institute of Masters of Wine in 1955.
Wine has been found in Egyptian tombs, with labels noting the vintage, the vineyard and the winemaker.
Ancient Greeks usually drank their wine mixed with water; drinking it neat was thought barbaric.
In ancient Rome, wine was often flavored with honey, herbs and even sea water.
The word 'vintage' simply means the year the grapes were picked.
Non-vintage Champagne blends several years so the house style tastes the same every year.
Rosé is usually made by leaving black grape skins in the juice for just a few hours.
In Champagne, rosé can be made by blending red and white wine, which is banned almost everywhere else in Europe.
Gewürztraminer often smells of lychee and roses; Gewürz means 'spice' in German.
Viognier nearly disappeared in the 1960s, with only a few hectares left in Condrieu.
Chenin Blanc can be dry, sweet or sparkling, and still or fortified-like, all from the Loire Valley.
Muscadet ages 'sur lie' on its yeast, which adds texture and a slight prickle.
Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé face each other across the Loire and both make Sauvignon Blanc.
Alsace wines are named after their grape, unlike most French wines, which are named after places.
Terroir is the French idea that a wine should taste of its place: soil, slope, climate and people.
Limestone soils, as in Burgundy, Champagne and Chablis, are prized for wines with fresh acidity.
Chablis grows on Kimmeridgian clay full of fossil oyster shells, 150 million years old.
Some sparkling wines are aged under the sea, where cold, dark and pressure are said to help them age.

wines.name: Champagne Brut
wines.summary: The benchmark sparkling wine: a blend of three grapes, second fermentation in bottle and long ageing on the lees.

wines.name: Blanc de Blancs Champagne
wines.summary: Champagne made only from Chardonnay, often from the chalky Côte des Blancs: taut, precise and long-lived.

wines.name: Chablis
wines.summary: Unoaked (or lightly oaked) Chardonnay from cool, chalky slopes in northern Burgundy: steely and mineral.

wines.name: Meursault
wines.summary: Rich, nutty white Burgundy from the Côte de Beaune, fermented and aged in oak barrels.

wines.name: Bourgogne Pinot Noir
wines.summary: Silky Pinot Noir from the Côte d'Or, where each village and vineyard shows a slightly different face.

wines.name: Beaujolais (cru)
wines.summary: Juicy, low-tannin Gamay; the ten crus such as Morgon and Fleurie are the most serious.

wines.name: Margaux
wines.summary: Left Bank Bordeaux on gravel soils: Cabernet-led, perfumed and elegant, built to age.

wines.name: Pauillac
wines.summary: Home of three first growths: powerful, tannic Cabernet blends with cassis and pencil shavings.

wines.name: Saint-Émilion
wines.summary: Right Bank Bordeaux on limestone and clay: Merlot-led, plush and plummy.

wines.name: Pomerol
wines.summary: A tiny Right Bank appellation on clay with iron: velvety, rich Merlot.

wines.name: Sauternes
wines.summary: Sweet white from grapes shrivelled by noble rot in the autumn mists of the Ciron and Garonne.

wines.name: Pessac-Léognan blanc
wines.summary: Barrel-fermented Sauvignon–Sémillon blends from the gravels south of Bordeaux city.

wines.name: Sancerre
wines.summary: Crisp Loire Sauvignon Blanc from chalk, flint and clay: the classic match for goat cheese.

wines.name: Pouilly-Fumé
wines.summary: Sancerre's neighbor across the Loire, often with a smoky, flinty note from silex soils.

wines.name: Vouvray
wines.summary: Chenin Blanc from Touraine tuffeau, made dry, off-dry, sweet or sparkling.

wines.name: Muscadet Sèvre et Maine
wines.summary: Bone-dry, salty white from the Atlantic end of the Loire, often aged 'sur lie' for texture.

wines.name: Chinon
wines.summary: Fresh, herbal Cabernet Franc from the Loire: red fruit with a touch of graphite and leaf.

wines.name: Alsace Riesling
wines.summary: Dry, full and mineral Riesling grown in the rain shadow of the Vosges.

wines.name: Alsace Gewürztraminer
wines.summary: Pungent, low-acid and often off-dry: the most perfumed white of all.

wines.name: Côte-Rôtie
wines.summary: Steep northern Rhône Syrah, sometimes co-fermented with a little Viognier for perfume.

wines.name: Hermitage
wines.summary: A granite hill above Tain: the most powerful, long-lived Syrah of the northern Rhône.

wines.name: Condrieu
wines.summary: The original Viognier: heady apricot and blossom, rich texture, low acidity.

wines.name: Châteauneuf-du-Pape
wines.summary: The classic GSM: Grenache-led southern Rhône blend from galets-strewn vineyards; 13 grape varieties are allowed.

wines.name: Côtes du Rhône
wines.summary: An everyday GSM blend: generous red fruit and a touch of spice.

wines.name: Tavel rosé
wines.summary: France's only all-rosé appellation: deeper colored and more structured than most rosés.

wines.name: Provence rosé
wines.summary: Pale, dry and fresh: the style that made rosé fashionable around the world.

wines.name: Barolo
wines.summary: The 'king of wines' from Piedmont: pale in color but high in tannin and acidity, aged for years.

wines.name: Barbaresco
wines.summary: Barolo's neighbor: Nebbiolo that is often a little more approachable and perfumed.

wines.name: Barbera d'Asti
wines.summary: Juicy, high-acid and low-tannin red: Piedmont's everyday wine.

wines.name: Moscato d'Asti
wines.summary: Gently sparkling, sweet and only about 5% alcohol: grapes in a glass.

wines.name: Gavi
wines.summary: Crisp, delicate Cortese from southern Piedmont.

wines.name: Chianti Classico
wines.summary: Sangiovese from the hills between Florence and Siena, marked by the black rooster.

wines.name: Brunello di Montalcino
wines.summary: 100% Sangiovese from warm, dry Montalcino; at least five years before release.

wines.name: Bolgheri (Super Tuscan)
wines.summary: Bordeaux varieties on the Tuscan coast: the home of the original Super Tuscans.

wines.name: Amarone della Valpolicella
wines.summary: Dry, powerful red from grapes dried for months before pressing (appassimento).

wines.name: Prosecco Superiore
wines.summary: Fresh, fruity sparkling wine made by the tank method in the hills of Conegliano Valdobbiadene.

wines.name: Soave Classico
wines.summary: Garganega from volcanic hills east of Verona: almond, pear and a saline finish.

wines.name: Sicilian Nero d'Avola
wines.summary: Sicily's signature red grape: ripe, dark fruit with fresh acidity from the island's hills.

wines.name: Rioja Reserva
wines.summary: Tempranillo-led blend aged at least three years, one in oak: the classic vanilla-and-strawberry Rioja.

wines.name: Ribera del Duero
wines.summary: Tempranillo (Tinto Fino) from a high, extreme plateau: dark, firm and concentrated.

wines.name: Priorat
wines.summary: Old-vine Garnacha and Cariñena on steep slate (llicorella) terraces in Catalonia.

wines.name: Rías Baixas Albariño
wines.summary: Fresh, saline Albariño from rainy, Atlantic Galicia.

wines.name: Rueda Verdejo
wines.summary: Zesty, herbal Verdejo from the high plains of Castilla y León.

wines.name: Cava
wines.summary: Traditional-method sparkling wine, mostly from Penedès, with Macabeo, Xarel·lo and Parellada.

wines.name: Fino sherry
wines.summary: Bone-dry sherry aged under a layer of flor yeast in the solera.

wines.name: Pedro Ximénez sherry
wines.summary: Sun-dried PX grapes make an intensely sweet, syrupy, almost black sherry.

wines.name: Vinho Verde
wines.summary: Light, sometimes slightly spritzy white from Portugal's green north-west (Alvarinho, Loureiro).

wines.name: Douro red
wines.summary: Dry reds from the terraced schist valley of the Douro, the same grapes as port.

wines.name: Vintage Port
wines.summary: Fortified wine from a declared great year, bottled young and aged for decades in bottle.

wines.name: 20 Year Old Tawny
wines.summary: Port aged in small casks until it turns amber, nutty and mellow.

wines.name: Madeira (Malmsey)
wines.summary: Heated and oxidized fortified wine from the island of Madeira; practically indestructible.

wines.name: Mosel Riesling Kabinett
wines.summary: Light, off-dry Riesling from steep slate slopes: low alcohol, electric acidity.

wines.name: Rheingau Riesling trocken
wines.summary: Dry, firm Riesling from south-facing slopes above the Rhine.

wines.name: Trockenbeerenauslese
wines.summary: Made from individually picked botrytized berries: rare, intensely sweet, with racy acidity.

wines.name: Wachau Grüner Veltliner
wines.summary: Austria's signature white: peppery, citrusy and sometimes rich, from Danube terraces.

wines.name: Blaufränkisch
wines.summary: Spicy, fresh Austrian red from Burgenland.

wines.name: Tokaji Aszú
wines.summary: Hungary's legendary sweet wine from botrytized Furmint berries ('aszú').

wines.name: Santorini Assyrtiko
wines.summary: Bone-dry, salty white from basket-trained vines on volcanic soils.

wines.name: Napa Valley Cabernet
wines.summary: Ripe, opulent Cabernet from California's most famous valley.

wines.name: Sonoma Coast Chardonnay
wines.summary: Cool-climate Californian Chardonnay, often barrel-fermented with malolactic conversion.

wines.name: Lodi Zinfandel
wines.summary: Jammy, high-alcohol old-vine Zinfandel from California's Central Valley.

wines.name: Willamette Valley Pinot Noir
wines.summary: Oregon's cool-climate Pinot Noir: bright red fruit and earthy depth.

wines.name: Mendoza Malbec
wines.summary: High-altitude Argentine Malbec: deep purple, plush and generous.

wines.name: Salta Torrontés
wines.summary: Floral white from some of the world's highest vineyards.

wines.name: Colchagua Carmenère
wines.summary: Chile's signature grape, once mistaken for Merlot: dark fruit and a green-pepper note.

wines.name: Barossa Shiraz
wines.summary: Rich, ripe Australian Shiraz, often from very old vines.

wines.name: Clare Valley Riesling
wines.summary: Dry, lime-scented Riesling that develops toast and petrol notes with age.

wines.name: Hunter Valley Sémillon
wines.summary: Picked early at about 11% alcohol, unoaked, yet turns honeyed and toasty after years in bottle.

wines.name: Coonawarra Cabernet
wines.summary: Cabernet from the famous strip of red 'terra rossa' soil.

wines.name: Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc
wines.summary: The pungent, passion-fruit style that put New Zealand on the wine map.

wines.name: Central Otago Pinot Noir
wines.summary: The world's southernmost wine region: vivid, fruity Pinot Noir.

wines.name: Stellenbosch Cabernet
wines.summary: Structured Cape Cabernet, between Old and New World in style.

wines.name: Swartland Chenin Blanc
wines.summary: Old-vine, dry-farmed Chenin: textured, honeyed and fresh.

wines.name: Pinotage
wines.summary: South Africa's own crossing of Pinot Noir and Cinsault.

wines.name: Bekaa Valley red
wines.summary: High-altitude Lebanese blends, famous since Château Musar: spicy, savory and long-lived.

wines.name: Lebanese Obaideh
wines.summary: A native Lebanese white, also used for arak: fresh, nutty and lightly floral.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.summary: The world's most versatile white grape. A blank canvas that shows its place and its winemaker: steely in Chablis, creamy and oaky in California, toasty in Champagne.
grapes.cool: Green apple, lemon and wet stones with high acidity: Chablis, Champagne, Tasmania.
grapes.warm: Peach, pineapple and banana with fuller body; often oaked: California, Australia.
grapes.styles: From unoaked and crisp (Chablis, Mâcon) to rich, oaked and buttery with malolactic conversion. Also the backbone of Blanc de Blancs Champagne.
grapes.ageing: Most are best within 3–5 years. Top white Burgundy can develop for 10–20 years, gaining nutty, honeyed notes.
grapes.fact: Chardonnay is the result of a cross between Pinot Noir and the obscure Gouais Blanc, a grape medieval nobles tried to ban.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.summary: Zesty, aromatic and instantly recognizable: high acidity with green, herbaceous aromas and citrus or tropical fruit.
grapes.cool: Gooseberry, grass and flint; lean and mineral: Sancerre, Pouilly-Fumé.
grapes.warm: Passion fruit, melon and riper citrus: Marlborough, parts of Chile and South Africa.
grapes.styles: Usually unoaked and best young. In Bordeaux it is blended with Sémillon for dry whites (sometimes oaked) and for sweet Sauternes. Oaked California versions are called Fumé Blanc.
grapes.ageing: Drink young, within 1–3 years. Oaked white Bordeaux can age longer.
grapes.fact: Sauvignon Blanc is a parent of Cabernet Sauvignon, after a chance crossing with Cabernet Franc in 17th-century Bordeaux.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.summary: Thrillingly high acidity and intense aromas of citrus, stone fruit and flowers. Made bone dry to lusciously sweet, and one of the longest-lived whites.
grapes.cool: Green apple, lime and blossom; often off-dry with low alcohol: Mosel.
grapes.warm: Riper peach and citrus, drier and fuller: Alsace, Clare and Eden Valley (lime), Pfalz.
grapes.styles: Never oaked for flavor. Dry (Trocken, Grosses Gewächs), off-dry (Kabinett), sweet (Spätlese, Auslese) and noble-rot or ice wines (Beerenauslese, Trockenbeerenauslese, Eiswein).
grapes.ageing: Exceptional. Good examples evolve for decades, developing honey, toast and the famous petrol note.
grapes.fact: The petrol aroma in aged Riesling comes from a compound called TDN, which builds up with sun exposure and age.

grapes.name: Pinot Grigio
grapes.origin: Burgundy, France (a color mutation of Pinot Noir)
grapes.summary: Two styles from one grape: light, crisp and neutral as Italian Pinot Grigio, or rich, spicy and textured as Alsace Pinot Gris.
grapes.cool: Pinot Grigio style: light, crisp, lemon and pear: northern Italy (Veneto, Friuli, Alto Adige).
grapes.warm: Pinot Gris style: fuller, honeyed, stone fruit and spice, sometimes off-dry: Alsace, Oregon, New Zealand.
grapes.styles: Unoaked. Its skins are pinkish-grey, so long skin contact gives copper-tinted 'ramato' wines.
grapes.ageing: Pinot Grigio is for drinking young; Alsace Pinot Gris can age for a decade.
grapes.fact: 'Grigio' and 'Gris' both mean grey, after the grape's dusky pink-grey skin.

grapes.name: Chenin Blanc
grapes.summary: A chameleon with piercing acidity, made in every style: dry, off-dry, sweet and sparkling. Honeyed, apple-scented and capable of great age.
grapes.cool: Green apple, quince and wet wool; often off-dry or sparkling: Vouvray, Savennières.
grapes.warm: Riper tropical and stone fruit, often oaked: South Africa (Swartland, Stellenbosch).
grapes.styles: Dry (sec), off-dry (demi-sec), sweet (moelleux, often with botrytis) and traditional-method sparkling (Crémant de Loire). South Africa's most planted grape, where it is also called Steen.
grapes.ageing: Top Loire Chenin, dry or sweet, can age for 20–50 years.

grapes.name: Sémillon
grapes.summary: Low in aroma when young but rich in texture. The heart of Sauternes, and in Australia's Hunter Valley a unique dry wine that ages into toast and honey.
grapes.cool: Hunter Valley: picked early at about 11% abv, lemon and grass, ageing to toast and honey.
grapes.warm: Riper, waxy and fuller; susceptible to noble rot in Sauternes.
grapes.styles: Blended with Sauvignon Blanc in dry white Bordeaux and in Sauternes and Barsac. Thin skins make it prone to botrytis.
grapes.ageing: Sauternes and Hunter Sémillon both age for decades.

grapes.name: Gewürztraminer
grapes.summary: The most perfumed grape of all: rose petals, lychee and ginger. Low acidity, deep color and an oily texture.
grapes.styles: Dry to sweet; in Alsace also late-harvest (Vendanges Tardives) and botrytized (Sélection de Grains Nobles).
grapes.ageing: Mostly drink young; sweet Alsace versions age well.
grapes.fact: 'Gewürz' means spice in German; the grape is pink-skinned and its wines can look golden even when young.

grapes.name: Muscat
grapes.origin: Ancient Mediterranean; a family of related grapes
grapes.summary: The one grape whose wine smells exactly of grapes. Floral, peachy and orange-scented, from feather-light Moscato d'Asti to syrupy Rutherglen Muscat.
grapes.styles: Sparkling and sweet (Asti), fortified (Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise, Rutherglen Muscat), dry (Alsace) and sweet passito.
grapes.ageing: Drink young, except fortified styles like Rutherglen Muscat.

grapes.name: Viognier
grapes.summary: Full-bodied and heady with apricot, peach and honeysuckle. Low acidity, high alcohol and a silky texture.
grapes.styles: Condrieu is the benchmark. A small amount is co-fermented with Syrah in Côte-Rôtie for color stability and perfume.
grapes.ageing: Best young, within about 3 years.
grapes.fact: In the 1960s Condrieu was down to about 8 hectares and Viognier nearly vanished.

grapes.name: Albariño
grapes.summary: Fresh, saline and aromatic: peach, grapefruit and a sea-breeze tang. The seafood wine of the Atlantic coast.
grapes.styles: Usually unoaked, sometimes lees-aged for texture. As Alvarinho it makes Portugal's finest Vinho Verde in Monção and Melgaço.
grapes.ageing: Drink within 2–4 years.

grapes.name: Grüner Veltliner
grapes.summary: Austria's signature white: crisp green fruit with a twist of white pepper.
grapes.styles: From light, peppery everyday wines (Weinviertel DAC) to powerful, age-worthy Smaragd from the Wachau.
grapes.ageing: Simple ones young; top single-vineyard wines age 10+ years.

grapes.name: Torrontés
grapes.origin: Argentina (a cross of Muscat of Alexandria and Criolla Chica)
grapes.summary: Argentina's aromatic white: exuberantly floral like Muscat, but dry, with a bitter-citrus finish.
grapes.styles: Best from high-altitude vineyards in Salta (Cafayate), where cool nights keep acidity.

grapes.name: Furmint
grapes.summary: The great grape of Tokaj: searing acidity, smoky minerality and a strong affinity for noble rot.
grapes.styles: Tokaji Aszú (sweet, botrytized), Szamorodni, late harvest and increasingly fine dry Furmint.
grapes.ageing: Aszú can age for a century.

grapes.name: Assyrtiko
grapes.summary: Bone-dry, mineral and saline, keeping high acidity even in hot sun. Grown on Santorini in basket-shaped vines (kouloura).
grapes.styles: Dry, sometimes oaked (Nykteri); sweet Vinsanto from sun-dried grapes.
grapes.fact: Santorini's vines are ungrafted; phylloxera cannot survive in its volcanic sand.

grapes.name: Melon de Bourgogne
grapes.summary: The neutral grape behind Muscadet: light, lemony and briny, often given texture by ageing on its lees (sur lie).
grapes.styles: Muscadet Sèvre et Maine sur lie: bottled straight off the lees for freshness and a light yeasty note.

grapes.name: Garganega
grapes.summary: The grape of Soave: almond, lemon and white flowers, with a gentle, textured finish.
grapes.styles: Soave Classico from volcanic hills; sweet Recioto di Soave from dried grapes.

grapes.name: Glera
grapes.summary: The grape of Prosecco: light, fresh, with pear, apple and white flowers.
grapes.styles: Tank-method sparkling (spumante) and gently sparkling (frizzante).

grapes.name: Verdejo
grapes.summary: Rueda's grape: herbaceous and citrusy with a slightly bitter almond finish.
grapes.styles: Usually unoaked and fresh; often blended with Sauvignon Blanc.

grapes.name: Cortese
grapes.summary: The grape of Gavi: delicate, crisp and lemony with a hint of almond.

grapes.name: Verdicchio
grapes.summary: Central Italy's finest white: high acidity, lemon, green almond and a gently bitter finish; ages surprisingly well.

grapes.name: Fiano
grapes.summary: Waxy, nutty and honeyed southern Italian white with good acidity. Best from Fiano di Avellino.

grapes.name: Greco
grapes.summary: Greco di Tufo: firm, mineral and peachy with bright acidity and a light phenolic grip.

grapes.name: Palomino
grapes.summary: A neutral, low-acid grape that is the perfect base for Sherry, where flor and oxygen create the flavors.
grapes.styles: All dry Sherry styles: Fino, Manzanilla, Amontillado, Palo Cortado, Oloroso.

grapes.name: Pedro Ximénez
grapes.summary: Sun-dried in Jerez and Montilla to make PX: black, syrupy and intensely raisined.

grapes.name: Marsanne & Roussanne
grapes.summary: Rhône partners: Marsanne brings body and nutty richness, Roussanne aroma and acidity. White Hermitage is their peak.
grapes.ageing: White Hermitage can age for decades.

grapes.name: Trebbiano
grapes.summary: High-yielding and neutral with high acidity. Across Italy it makes simple whites; in France, as Ugni Blanc, it is distilled into Cognac and Armagnac.

grapes.name: Vermentino
grapes.summary: Herbal, citrusy and saline: the Mediterranean seaside white of Sardinia, Liguria, coastal Tuscany and Provence (as Rolle).

grapes.name: Pinot Blanc
grapes.origin: Burgundy, France (a mutation of Pinot Noir)
grapes.summary: Gentle, round and apple-scented, a softer cousin of Chardonnay. Widely used for Crémant d'Alsace.

grapes.name: Macabeo
grapes.summary: The main white grape of Rioja (as Viura) and a key Cava grape. Neutral and fresh, or nutty when aged in old oak.
grapes.styles: Fresh young white Rioja, oxidatively aged traditional white Rioja, and Cava (with Xarel·lo and Parellada).

grapes.name: Silvaner
grapes.summary: Earthy, herbal and quietly mineral; at its best in Franken, bottled in the squat Bocksbeutel flask.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.summary: The king of red grapes: small, thick-skinned berries give deep color, high tannin and blackcurrant fruit. Built to age, especially with oak.
grapes.cool: Leaner, with herbaceous green bell pepper and leafy notes; needs a warm site to ripen.
grapes.warm: Riper black fruit, often mint or eucalyptus, fuller body: Napa, Coonawarra, Margaret River.
grapes.styles: Often blended (Bordeaux blend) with Merlot and Cabernet Franc, which soften and add aroma. Usually matured in oak.
grapes.ageing: Top examples develop over 10–30 years: cedar, tobacco, leather, forest floor.
grapes.fact: Cabernet Sauvignon ripens late, which is why it does best on the warm, free-draining gravel of Bordeaux's Left Bank.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.summary: Plush and approachable: red and black plum, softer tannins and fuller body than Cabernet. The main grape of Bordeaux's Right Bank.
grapes.cool: Strawberry, red plum and herbal hints; medium body: Bordeaux in cool years, northern Italy.
grapes.warm: Black plum and blackberry, fuller body, softer acidity: Chile, California, Australia.
grapes.styles: From easy-drinking and fruity to some of the world's most expensive wines (Pétrus). Blended with Cabernet Franc on the Right Bank.
grapes.ageing: Most drink well within 5 years; top Pomerol and Saint-Émilion age for decades.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.summary: Light in color and tannin, high in acidity, haunting in aroma. Fragile and hard to grow, but sublime when it works.
grapes.cool: Cranberry, red cherry and earthy notes; high acidity: Burgundy, Germany, Oregon.
grapes.warm: Riper black cherry, plum and spice; fuller body: Central Otago, California, Chile.
grapes.styles: Still red from Burgundy and the New World; a key grape in Champagne and other traditional-method sparkling wines. Sometimes whole-bunch fermented.
grapes.ageing: Grand cru Burgundy can age 20+ years, gaining forest floor, mushroom and game.
grapes.fact: Pinot Noir mutates easily: Pinot Gris and Pinot Blanc are its color mutations.

grapes.name: Syrah
grapes.summary: Deep, spicy and dark-fruited. In the Rhône it is savory and peppery; as Australian Shiraz, ripe, rich and chocolatey.
grapes.cool: Syrah style: black pepper, violet, blackberry and savory meat: Northern Rhône, Hawke's Bay.
grapes.warm: Shiraz style: ripe blackberry, plum, chocolate and sweet spice: Barossa, McLaren Vale.
grapes.styles: Single varietal or blended (GSM with Grenache and Mourvèdre; with Cabernet in Australia). Also sparkling Shiraz in Australia.
grapes.ageing: Hermitage and top Barossa age 15–30 years.

grapes.name: Grenache
grapes.summary: Thin-skinned and generous: high alcohol, soft tannin, ripe strawberry and raspberry with white pepper and herbs. Loves heat and wind.
grapes.styles: The backbone of Southern Rhône blends (GSM) and Priorat; excellent rosé (Tavel, Navarra, Provence) and fortified wines (Banyuls).
grapes.ageing: Most drink young; Châteauneuf-du-Pape and Priorat age 10–20 years.

grapes.name: Tempranillo
grapes.summary: Spain's noble grape: red cherry, plum and leather, with vanilla and coconut from traditional American oak.
grapes.styles: Rioja and Ribera del Duero age categories: Joven, Crianza, Reserva, Gran Reserva. A component of Port (as Tinta Roriz).
grapes.ageing: Gran Reserva Rioja can age for decades.
grapes.fact: The name comes from 'temprano', early: it ripens weeks before many other Spanish grapes.

grapes.name: Sangiovese
grapes.summary: Italy's most planted grape: sour cherry, tomato leaf and dried herbs, with high acidity and firm tannin. Made for food.
grapes.styles: Chianti, Brunello di Montalcino (100% Sangiovese), Vino Nobile di Montepulciano and Super Tuscans (often with Cabernet or Merlot).
grapes.ageing: Brunello and Chianti Classico Riserva age 10–25 years.
grapes.fact: The name is said to come from 'sanguis Jovis', the blood of Jupiter.

grapes.name: Nebbiolo
grapes.summary: Tar and roses: pale in color yet ferociously high in tannin and acidity. The grape of Barolo and Barbaresco.
grapes.styles: Barolo and Barbaresco DOCG; lighter Langhe Nebbiolo; Valtellina in Lombardy.
grapes.ageing: Barolo often needs 10+ years and can age for 50; it fades early to garnet.
grapes.fact: Named after 'nebbia', the fog that blankets the Langhe hills at harvest in October.

grapes.name: Malbec
grapes.summary: Inky purple with ripe blackberry, plum and violet. Velvety tannins make Argentine Malbec one of the world's most loved reds.
grapes.styles: Argentina: ripe, plush, often oaked; high-altitude sites give more freshness. Cahors: firmer and more rustic.
grapes.ageing: Most best within 5–8 years; top examples longer.
grapes.fact: Once a major Bordeaux grape, Malbec almost disappeared there after the 1956 frost, while it flourished in Argentina.

grapes.name: Zinfandel
grapes.summary: Jammy and generous: blackberry, raspberry jam and sweet spice with high alcohol. California's heritage grape and Puglia's Primitivo.
grapes.styles: Big oaked reds, old-vine Zinfandel, and off-dry pink 'White Zinfandel'. Ripens unevenly, so bunches can contain raisins and green berries together.

grapes.name: Cabernet Franc
grapes.summary: Lighter and more fragrant than its offspring Cabernet Sauvignon: red fruit, violet and a leafy, green pepper note.
grapes.styles: Single-varietal in the Loire (Chinon, Bourgueil, Saumur-Champigny); blending partner in Bordeaux (Cheval Blanc is mostly Cabernet Franc).

grapes.name: Gamay
grapes.summary: The grape of Beaujolais: juicy, light and fragrant with red cherry, raspberry and banana. Best slightly chilled.
grapes.styles: Beaujolais Nouveau (carbonic maceration, released weeks after harvest), Beaujolais-Villages and the ten crus (Morgon, Fleurie, Moulin-à-Vent).
grapes.ageing: Mostly young; top crus like Morgon and Moulin-à-Vent age 5–10 years.
grapes.fact: In 1395 Duke Philip the Bold banned Gamay from Burgundy's best slopes, calling it 'very bad and very disloyal'.

grapes.name: Pinotage
grapes.summary: South Africa's own grape: dark fruit with smoky, earthy notes. Modern versions can be juicy or coffee-scented.
grapes.styles: From light and fruity to oaked, age-worthy wines; also blended in 'Cape blends'.

grapes.name: Carmenère
grapes.summary: Chile's signature grape: red and black fruit with green pepper, paprika and herbs. Late ripening and soft.
grapes.fact: Believed extinct after phylloxera, it was rediscovered in Chile in 1994, where it had been mistaken for Merlot for over a century.

grapes.name: Barbera
grapes.summary: Deep in color but low in tannin, with mouthwatering acidity and juicy black cherry: Piedmont's everyday red.

grapes.name: Dolcetto
grapes.summary: 'Little sweet one', yet dry: soft acidity, grippy tannin, black cherry and bitter almond. Drunk young in Piedmont.

grapes.name: Montepulciano
grapes.summary: Deeply colored, plummy and soft: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo. Not to be confused with the Tuscan town of Montepulciano.

grapes.name: Aglianico
grapes.summary: 'The Barolo of the South': very high tannin and acidity, black fruit, smoke and leather. From volcanic soils in Taurasi and Vulture.

grapes.name: Nero d'Avola
grapes.summary: Sicily's star red: ripe black cherry and plum, medium acidity and soft-to-firm tannins.

grapes.name: Corvina
grapes.summary: The main grape of Valpolicella and Amarone: sour cherry and almond when fresh, dried cherry and chocolate when dried (appassimento).
grapes.styles: Valpolicella (light), Ripasso (refermented on Amarone skins), Amarone (dry, from dried grapes) and Recioto (sweet).

grapes.name: Mourvèdre
grapes.summary: Thick-skinned and sun-loving: blackberry, game, leather and herbs, with high tannin. The 'M' in GSM.
grapes.styles: Bandol in Provence is its home; Jumilla in Spain (as Monastrell); Australia (as Mataro).

grapes.name: Carignan
grapes.summary: High in acidity, tannin and color. Once a bulk grape; old bush vines in Priorat, Languedoc and Chile now make serious wines.

grapes.name: Cinsault
grapes.summary: Light, fragrant and low in tannin: strawberry and flowers. Important in rosé and as a parent of Pinotage.

grapes.name: Touriga Nacional
grapes.summary: Portugal's finest black grape: deep, floral and concentrated, with violet, blackberry and firm tannin. A key Port grape.
grapes.styles: Port and dry Douro and Dão reds, usually in blends with Touriga Franca and Tinta Roriz.

grapes.name: Petit Verdot
grapes.summary: A late-ripening Bordeaux blending grape: inky color, violet and spice, firm tannins. Used in small amounts for structure.

grapes.name: Mencía
grapes.summary: Fragrant, fresh and medium-bodied: red cherry, blackberry and herbs from steep slate slopes in Bierzo.

grapes.name: Blaufränkisch
grapes.summary: Austria's serious red: dark cherry, pepper and mineral, with bright acidity and firm tannin.

grapes.name: Zweigelt
grapes.summary: Austria's most planted red: juicy red cherry, soft tannins and fresh acidity.

grapes.name: Xinomavro
grapes.summary: 'Acid-black': pale, high in acidity and tannin, with tomato, olive and red fruit. Often compared to Nebbiolo.

grapes.name: Agiorgitiko
grapes.summary: 'St George's grape': soft, plummy and spicy, from medium to full bodied depending on altitude.

grapes.name: Tannat
grapes.summary: As its name suggests, fiercely tannic: black fruit, spice and smoke. Madiran's grape and Uruguay's flagship.
grapes.fact: Tannat has some of the highest levels of procyanidins (a type of antioxidant) of any wine grape.

grapes.name: Negroamaro
grapes.summary: 'Black-bitter': dark plum, earth and a bitter twist, from the heel of Italy (Salice Salentino).

grapes.name: Baga
grapes.summary: High-acid, high-tannin grape of Bairrada, for age-worthy reds and fine traditional-method sparkling wines.

grapes.name: Meunier
grapes.summary: Champagne's third grape: buds late and ripens early, avoiding frost. Adds fruity roundness to young Champagne.
grapes.fact: 'Meunier' means miller: the undersides of its leaves are dusted with fine white hairs, as if floured.

grapes.name: Obaideh
grapes.summary: Lebanon's best-known native white grape: soft, round and gently aromatic, often compared to Chardonnay. Used in dry whites and to distil arak.

grapes.name: Merwah
grapes.summary: Ancient mountain grape from Mount Lebanon, often linked to Sémillon. Waxy texture, citrus and a light nutty finish; a key white in Château Musar's white.

regions.name: France
regions.climate: Cool continental in the north and east, maritime on the Atlantic coast, Mediterranean in the south.
regions.summary: The benchmark for almost every classic style. France's regions gave the world its most imitated grapes, its appellation system and the very idea of terroir.
regions.classification: **AOC/AOP** (Appellation d'Origine Contrôlée/Protégée) rules control where grapes grow, which varieties are allowed, yields and winemaking. **IGP** (Vin de Pays) gives more freedom; **Vin de France** is the most basic category.
facts: Labels usually name the place, not the grape: Sancerre is Sauvignon Blanc, red Burgundy is Pinot Noir.
Champagne, Bordeaux and Burgundy are among the most valuable wine regions on earth.
regions.history: Greeks planted vines at Marseille around 600 BC and the Romans spread them up the Rhône, to Bordeaux, Burgundy and the Loire. Medieval monks mapped the best plots; merchants and kings built the great names. Phylloxera ruined almost every vineyard in the 1870s–80s, and fraud that followed led to the AOC laws of 1935, the model for wine laws worldwide.

regions.name: Bordeaux
regions.climate: Moderate maritime, moderated by the Atlantic and the Gironde estuary; vintages vary with autumn rain.
regions.summary: The world's most famous red wine region: blends of Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot from châteaux on either side of the Gironde estuary, plus great sweet and dry whites.
regions.styles: Mostly red blends. **Left Bank** (Médoc, Graves): gravel soils, Cabernet Sauvignon-led. **Right Bank** (Saint-Émilion, Pomerol): clay and limestone, Merlot-led. Dry whites from Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon; sweet Sauternes.
regions.classification: The **1855 Classification** ranked Médoc (and one Graves) châteaux from First to Fifth Growth; Sauternes was ranked too. Saint-Émilion has its own classification, revised about every ten years. Pomerol has none.
facts: Blending spreads risk: Merlot ripens early, Cabernet Sauvignon late.
The five First Growths are Lafite, Latour, Margaux, Haut-Brion and Mouton Rothschild (promoted in 1973).
regions.history: Founded as Roman Burdigala, Bordeaux grew rich on trade: it belonged to the English crown from 1152 to 1453 and shipped 'claret' to London. In the 1600s Dutch engineers drained the Médoc, revealing the gravel where Cabernet thrives; estates such as Haut-Brion began selling wine by name. The 1855 classification, Émile Peynaud's scientific winemaking and the 1982 vintage made Bordeaux the world's benchmark for fine wine.

regions.name: Médoc
regions.summary: The northern, lower-lying part of the Left Bank peninsula. More clay and Merlot than the Haut-Médoc; good-value reds and many Crus Bourgeois.

regions.name: Haut-Médoc
regions.climate: Gravel ridges near the estuary drain well and store heat, helping late-ripening Cabernet.
regions.summary: The heart of the Left Bank, home to four famous communes and most of the 1855 classified growths.

regions.name: Saint-Estèphe
regions.summary: The northernmost famous commune: more clay, firmer and more rustic wines with high acidity and tannin. Cos d'Estournel and Montrose are leaders.

regions.name: Pauillac
regions.summary: Home of three First Growths (Lafite, Latour, Mouton). Powerful, long-lived Cabernet with blackcurrant, cedar and pencil shavings.

regions.name: Saint-Julien
regions.summary: Small and consistent: balanced, elegant, classic claret between Pauillac and Margaux. Léoville Las Cases, Ducru-Beaucaillou.

regions.name: Margaux
regions.summary: Thin gravel soils give the most perfumed, silky wines of the Médoc. Château Margaux is its First Growth.

regions.name: Pessac-Léognan
regions.summary: The northern Graves, on Bordeaux's doorstep. Smoky, earthy reds and the best oaked dry whites. Home of First Growth Haut-Brion.

regions.name: Graves
regions.summary: Named after its gravel soils, south of the city along the Garonne. Red and dry white wines.

regions.name: Sauternes & Barsac
regions.climate: Autumn mists from the cold Ciron river meeting the warmer Garonne encourage noble rot; sunny afternoons dry the grapes.
regions.summary: The world's most famous noble-rot sweet wines: golden, honeyed, with apricot, marmalade and great ageing potential. Château d'Yquem is the icon.
regions.styles: Grapes are picked in several passes (tries) through the vineyard, berry by berry.

regions.name: Entre-Deux-Mers
regions.summary: 'Between two seas': the land between the Garonne and Dordogne rivers. Fresh dry whites and plenty of Bordeaux AOC red.

regions.name: Saint-Émilion
regions.climate: Limestone plateau and clay slopes; cooler soils suit early-ripening Merlot.
regions.summary: A medieval hilltop town and UNESCO site on the Right Bank. Plush Merlot and Cabernet Franc blends from limestone and clay.
regions.classification: Saint-Émilion Grand Cru Classé, Premier Grand Cru Classé B and A, revised roughly every ten years.

regions.name: Pomerol
regions.summary: A tiny plateau of clay and gravel producing velvety, opulent Merlot, including Pétrus and Le Pin. No classification, yet some of the world's priciest reds.

regions.name: Fronsac
regions.summary: Hilly Right Bank appellation west of Libourne: sturdy, value Merlot.

regions.name: Castillon
regions.summary: Castillon Côtes de Bordeaux: limestone slopes east of Saint-Émilion, a source of value Merlot.

regions.name: Côtes de Bourg
regions.summary: Right bank of the Gironde opposite Margaux: robust, good-value Merlot-based reds.

regions.name: Blaye
regions.summary: Blaye Côtes de Bordeaux: rolling hills north of Bourg, fruity reds and some whites.

regions.name: Burgundy
regions.climate: Cool continental: cold winters, warm summers, risk of spring frost and hail. Vineyards face east and south-east for morning sun.
regions.summary: Terroir taken to its extreme: a narrow strip of slopes where Pinot Noir and Chardonnay change character from one vineyard to the next.
regions.styles: Red Burgundy (Pinot Noir), white Burgundy (Chardonnay), from crisp Chablis to rich Meursault. Crémant de Bourgogne sparkling.
regions.classification: A pyramid: **Regional** (Bourgogne) → **Village** (e.g. Gevrey-Chambertin) → **Premier Cru** → **Grand Cru** (33 vineyards, about 1–2% of production).
facts: Vineyards are split between many owners, so a Grand Cru like Clos de Vougeot has more than 80 producers.
A 'climat' is a precisely named vineyard plot; Burgundy's climats are a UNESCO World Heritage site.
regions.history: Benedictine and Cistercian monks spent centuries tasting each plot and walling the best, such as the Clos de Vougeot. The Dukes of Burgundy made its wine a diplomatic gift, and in 1395 Philip the Bold banned Gamay to protect Pinot Noir. The Revolution sold Church land and Napoleon's inheritance law split it among heirs, which is why vineyards today are divided among many small growers. UNESCO listed the climats in 2015.

regions.name: Chablis
regions.climate: The northernmost part of Burgundy: cool, with frost risk. Kimmeridgian limestone full of fossil oyster shells.
regions.summary: Steely, unoaked or lightly oaked Chardonnay: green apple, lemon and wet stones with high acidity. Petit Chablis, Chablis, Premier Cru and Grand Cru.

regions.name: Côte de Nuits
regions.summary: The northern half of the Côte d'Or and the home of great red Burgundy: Gevrey-Chambertin, Chambolle-Musigny, Vosne-Romanée (Romanée-Conti), Nuits-Saint-Georges.

regions.name: Côte de Beaune
regions.summary: The southern half of the Côte d'Or: the world's greatest Chardonnay in Meursault, Puligny- and Chassagne-Montrachet, plus fine reds from Pommard, Volnay and Corton.

regions.name: Côte Chalonnaise
regions.summary: Value Burgundy from villages such as Mercurey, Givry, Rully and Montagny; also Bouzeron (Aligoté).

regions.name: Mâconnais
regions.climate: Warmer and sunnier than the Côte d'Or.
regions.summary: Ripe, rounded, mostly unoaked Chardonnay: Mâcon-Villages and the richer Pouilly-Fuissé and Saint-Véran.

regions.name: Beaujolais
regions.climate: Semi-continental, warmer than Burgundy; granite hills in the north, clay and limestone in the south.
regions.summary: Gamay country: juicy, light reds from easy Beaujolais Nouveau to the serious granite-grown crus.
regions.styles: Beaujolais (often carbonic maceration), Beaujolais-Villages and ten crus, including Fleurie, Morgon and Moulin-à-Vent.
facts: Beaujolais Nouveau is released on the third Thursday of November, weeks after harvest.
regions.history: Gamay was banished from the Côte d'Or in 1395 and found its home on Beaujolais' granite hills. Lyon became its thirsty market. In the 1970s–80s Georges Duboeuf turned the November release of Beaujolais Nouveau into a worldwide event; today the ten crus are winning back respect.

regions.name: Jura
regions.summary: Quirky mountain region known for Vin Jaune, a Savagnin wine aged under a flor-like yeast for over six years, plus Vin de Paille and Crémant du Jura.

regions.name: Savoie
regions.summary: Alpine vineyards making crisp, light whites (Jacquère, Altesse) and reds (Mondeuse) perfect with fondue.

regions.name: Rhône Valley
regions.climate: North: moderate continental, steep granite slopes. South: Mediterranean, hot and dry, swept by the cold Mistral wind.
regions.summary: Two regions in one: the narrow, steep Northern Rhône devoted to Syrah, and the broad, sunny Southern Rhône of Grenache-based blends.
regions.styles: North: single-varietal Syrah (Hermitage, Côte-Rôtie), Viognier (Condrieu). South: GSM blends (Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Côtes du Rhône), rosé (Tavel) and sweet Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise.
regions.classification: Côtes du Rhône → Côtes du Rhône Villages → named villages → crus such as Gigondas and Châteauneuf-du-Pape.
facts: Châteauneuf-du-Pape allows 13 grape varieties.
Côte-Rôtie means 'roasted slope', after its steep sun-baked terraces.
regions.history: Romans planted the steep granite hills of Côte-Rôtie and Hermitage. In the 14th century the popes lived in Avignon and gave Châteauneuf-du-Pape its name. In the 1920s Baron Le Roy wrote rules for Châteauneuf that became the blueprint for France's appellation system.

regions.name: Côte-Rôtie
regions.summary: Perfumed, elegant Syrah from very steep terraces; up to 20% Viognier may be co-fermented for aroma and color.

regions.name: Condrieu
regions.summary: Viognier's spiritual home: heady apricot, peach and blossom, full-bodied and silky.

regions.name: Saint-Joseph
regions.summary: A long strip on the west bank: fresh, peppery Syrah and some white Marsanne-Roussanne.

regions.name: Hermitage
regions.summary: A single granite hill above Tain: powerful, long-lived Syrah and rich white Marsanne. One of France's greatest wines.

regions.name: Crozes-Hermitage
regions.summary: The largest Northern Rhône appellation, around Hermitage: fruity, peppery, approachable Syrah.

regions.name: Cornas
regions.summary: 100% Syrah from a warm granite amphitheater: dark, tannic and wild.

regions.name: Châteauneuf-du-Pape
regions.climate: Hot, dry and windy; famous large round stones (galets roulés) store the day's heat.
regions.summary: The Southern Rhône's flagship: rich, warm, Grenache-led blends with red fruit, herbs (garrigue) and spice.

regions.name: Gigondas
regions.summary: Grenache-based reds beneath the jagged Dentelles de Montmirail: robust and spicy.

regions.name: Vacqueyras
regions.summary: Gigondas' neighbor: generous, value Grenache blends.

regions.name: Tavel & Lirac
regions.summary: Tavel is France's only all-rosé appellation: deeper, fuller, food-friendly rosé. Lirac makes all three colors.

regions.name: Côtes du Rhône
regions.summary: The big regional appellation, mostly in the south: juicy, spicy red blends with great value.

regions.name: Loire Valley
regions.climate: Cool: maritime near the Atlantic, becoming continental inland.
regions.summary: France's longest river and a paradise of fresh, high-acid wines: Muscadet, Chenin Blanc, Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc.
regions.styles: Every style: crisp whites, sweet botrytized Chenin (Coteaux du Layon), light reds, rosé (Rosé d'Anjou) and sparkling (Crémant de Loire, Saumur).
regions.history: The 'Garden of France', lined with royal châteaux. The river carried wine to Paris and to Dutch merchants, who loved sweet Chenin Blanc from Anjou and Vouvray. Sancerre, once a red-wine village, was replanted with Sauvignon Blanc after phylloxera and became famous in Paris bistros in the 1960s–70s.

regions.name: Muscadet
regions.summary: Near the Atlantic, around Nantes: light, crisp, briny whites, often aged sur lie. The perfect oyster wine.

regions.name: Anjou
regions.summary: Dry and sweet Chenin Blanc (Coteaux du Layon, Quarts de Chaume, Bonnezeaux), reds and the famous off-dry Rosé d'Anjou.

regions.name: Savennières
regions.summary: Intense, mineral, long-lived dry Chenin Blanc from steep schist slopes.

regions.name: Saumur
regions.summary: Tuffeau limestone country: Saumur-Champigny reds, dry Chenin and lots of traditional-method sparkling wine.

regions.name: Chinon
regions.summary: Fragrant Cabernet Franc with raspberry, violet and pencil-shaving notes.

regions.name: Bourgueil
regions.summary: North-bank Cabernet Franc, slightly firmer than Chinon.

regions.name: Vouvray
regions.summary: Chenin Blanc in every style: sec, demi-sec, moelleux and sparkling, from tuffeau limestone near Tours.

regions.name: Montlouis-sur-Loire
regions.summary: Vouvray's neighbor across the river: lively Chenin, still and sparkling.

regions.name: Touraine
regions.summary: A large area around Tours making fresh, good-value Sauvignon Blanc, light reds and sparkling wines.

regions.name: Sancerre
regions.climate: Cool continental; chalk, flint (silex) and limestone soils.
regions.summary: The classic Sauvignon Blanc: citrus, gooseberry and flinty minerality, with high acidity. Also light Pinot Noir reds and rosés.

regions.name: Pouilly-Fumé
regions.summary: Across the river from Sancerre: Sauvignon Blanc with a smoky, flinty edge (fumé means smoked).

regions.name: Champagne
regions.climate: Cool continental at the northern limit of grape growing; chalk subsoil stores water and reflects light.
regions.summary: The home of the world's most celebrated sparkling wine, made by the traditional method from Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Meunier.
regions.styles: Non-vintage blends (the house style), vintage, Blanc de Blancs (Chardonnay only), Blanc de Noirs (black grapes only) and rosé. Sweetness from Brut Nature to Doux.
regions.classification: Villages are rated: 17 Grand Cru and 42 Premier Cru villages.
facts: Non-vintage Champagne must spend at least 15 months in bottle, 12 of them on lees; vintage at least 3 years.
Most Champagne is a blend of many villages and years, assembled by large houses.
regions.history: Still wines from Champagne were served at the coronations of French kings in Reims. Cold winters stopped fermentation and spring restarted it, so the wine was often fizzy by accident. Stronger English glass, Dom Pérignon's careful blending and the widow Clicquot's riddling (1816) turned an accident into a luxury. Riots in 1911 led to the strict borders of today's appellation.

regions.name: Montagne de Reims
regions.summary: A forested plateau between Reims and Épernay; Pinot Noir gives body and structure. Grand cru villages include Ambonnay, Bouzy and Verzenay.

regions.name: Vallée de la Marne
regions.summary: Valley slopes where frost-resistant Meunier dominates, giving fruity, approachable wines.

regions.name: Côte des Blancs
regions.summary: East-facing chalk slopes south of Épernay devoted to Chardonnay: the source of elegant Blanc de Blancs (Cramant, Avize, Le Mesnil-sur-Oger).

regions.name: Côte de Sézanne
regions.summary: A southern extension of the Côte des Blancs, with riper, rounder Chardonnay.

regions.name: Côte des Bar
regions.summary: Far to the south, nearer Chablis than Reims: Kimmeridgian soils and fruity Pinot Noir.

regions.name: Alsace
regions.climate: One of France's driest regions: the Vosges mountains block rain from the west, giving long, sunny, dry autumns.
regions.summary: German-influenced but French: aromatic, mostly dry varietal whites labeled by grape, in tall flute bottles.
regions.styles: Dry whites, late-harvest Vendanges Tardives and botrytized Sélection de Grains Nobles; Crémant d'Alsace.
regions.classification: Alsace AOC, Alsace Grand Cru (51 vineyards) and Crémant d'Alsace.
regions.history: Alsace changed hands between France and Germany four times between 1871 and 1945, which explains its German grape names, tall flute bottles and wines labeled by grape. After 1918 growers turned from bulk wine to quality; Grand Cru vineyards were defined from 1975.

regions.name: Provence
regions.climate: Warm, sunny Mediterranean with the Mistral wind.
regions.summary: Rosé capital of the world: pale, dry, delicate pink wines. Bandol makes powerful Mourvèdre reds.

regions.name: Languedoc-Roussillon
regions.climate: Hot, dry Mediterranean.
regions.summary: France's largest vineyard area, from value varietal IGP Pays d'Oc wines to characterful blends from Minervois, Corbières and Faugères, and sweet Vins Doux Naturels in Roussillon.

regions.name: South West France
regions.summary: A patchwork of local grapes and styles: Cahors (Malbec), Madiran (Tannat), Bergerac (Bordeaux varieties) and Jurançon (sweet and dry whites).

regions.name: Italy
regions.climate: Alpine north, Mediterranean south; the Apennine mountains and the sea moderate the heat almost everywhere.
regions.summary: Wine is made in every one of Italy's 20 regions, with hundreds of native grapes. Its wines are made for the table: high acidity, savory and food-friendly.
