regions.classification: **DOCG** (strictest, guaranteed) → **DOC** → **IGT** (regional, more flexible, home of many Super Tuscans) → Vino. Classico marks a historic heartland; Riserva means longer ageing; Superiore, higher alcohol or stricter rules.
regions.history: Greeks called southern Italy Oenotria, 'land of vines'; the Etruscans and then Rome turned wine into an industry. Families such as the Antinori have made wine for 600 years. Italy's DOC laws arrived in 1963; the Super Tuscan rebels of the 1970s forced them to modernize, and today Italy grows more native grapes than any other country.

regions.name: Piedmont
regions.climate: Continental, at the foot of the Alps; fog in autumn; hillside vineyards for sun exposure.
regions.summary: Italy's most Burgundian region: hillside vineyards around Alba in the Langhe, home to Barolo and Barbaresco, plus everyday Barbera and Dolcetto and sweet Moscato d'Asti.
regions.history: Nebbiolo was long made sweet and slightly fizzy. In the mid-1800s the Marchesa Falletti of Barolo and Count Cavour hired the French winemaker Louis Oudart, who made it dry and age-worthy: Barolo became 'the wine of kings, the king of wines', the favorite of the House of Savoy. Since the 1980s, 'modernists' with small barrels and 'traditionalists' with big casks have argued over its style.

regions.name: Barolo
regions.summary: 'King of wines': 100% Nebbiolo, aged at least 38 months (18 in wood). Tar and roses, high tannin and acidity, decades of life.
facts: Single vineyards (MGA) such as Cannubi and Brunate are now named on labels, like Burgundy crus.

regions.name: Barbaresco
regions.summary: Barolo's neighbor: Nebbiolo that is often slightly more elegant and approachable earlier; at least 26 months' ageing.

regions.name: Roero
regions.summary: North of the Tanaro river: sandy soils give lighter, fragrant Nebbiolo and white Arneis.

regions.name: Dogliani
regions.summary: The home of serious Dolcetto.

regions.name: Barbera d'Asti
regions.summary: Juicy, high-acid, low-tannin Barbera around Asti, from everyday to oak-aged Nizza.

regions.name: Asti & Moscato d'Asti
regions.summary: Sweet, low-alcohol, grapey sparklers from Moscato Bianco.

regions.name: Gavi
regions.summary: Crisp, lemony whites from the Cortese grape.

regions.name: Tuscany
regions.climate: Warm Mediterranean, cooled by altitude inland and sea breezes on the coast.
regions.summary: Sangiovese's heartland: Chianti, Brunello di Montalcino and Vino Nobile, plus the coastal Super Tuscans of Bolgheri.
facts: Super Tuscans began in the 1970s when producers used Cabernet and Merlot outside DOC rules; Sassicaia now has its own DOC.
regions.history: Cosimo III de' Medici drew Chianti's borders in 1716, and Baron Ricasoli wrote its Sangiovese recipe in 1872. When the rules allowed thin, white-grape-heavy blends, rebels made Super Tuscans: Sassicaia (1968) and Tignanello (1971). Brunello di Montalcino was created by the Biondi-Santi family in the late 1800s.

regions.name: Chianti
regions.summary: A large DOCG around Florence and Siena: tart cherry, herbs and high acidity; at least 70% Sangiovese.

regions.name: Chianti Classico
regions.summary: The historic heart of Chianti between Florence and Siena, marked by the black rooster. Min. 80% Sangiovese; Riserva and Gran Selezione above.

regions.name: Brunello di Montalcino
regions.summary: 100% Sangiovese from a warm hilltop town south of Siena; released five years after harvest. Powerful and age-worthy. Rosso di Montalcino is its younger sibling.

regions.name: Vino Nobile di Montepulciano
regions.summary: Sangiovese (here called Prugnolo Gentile) from the hill town of Montepulciano. Not to be confused with the Montepulciano grape.

regions.name: Bolgheri
regions.summary: Coastal home of Super Tuscans: Bordeaux varieties such as Sassicaia, Ornellaia and Masseto.

regions.name: Maremma
regions.summary: Warm southern coast: ripe Morellino di Scansano (Sangiovese) and Vermentino.

regions.name: Carmignano
regions.summary: Historically blended Cabernet with Sangiovese long before the Super Tuscans.

regions.name: San Gimignano
regions.summary: The town of towers, known for Vernaccia di San Gimignano, a crisp, almondy white.

regions.name: Veneto
regions.summary: Italy's biggest-volume region: Prosecco, Soave, Valpolicella and Amarone, and oceans of Pinot Grigio.
regions.styles: Amarone della Valpolicella: dry, powerful wine from grapes dried for months (appassimento). Ripasso: Valpolicella refermented on Amarone skins.

regions.name: Trentino-Alto Adige
regions.summary: Alpine valleys with German and Italian heritage: pure, aromatic whites and Trentodoc sparkling wines.

regions.name: Friuli
regions.summary: North-east corner bordering Slovenia: Italy's finest whites, and pioneering skin-contact orange wines.

regions.name: Lombardy
regions.summary: Home to Franciacorta, Italy's top traditional-method sparkling wine, and to Alpine Nebbiolo in Valtellina.

regions.name: Emilia-Romagna
regions.summary: Food heaven (Parma ham, Parmigiano) and home of fizzy red Lambrusco.

regions.name: Umbria
regions.summary: Green heart of Italy: Orvieto whites and the tannic Sagrantino di Montefalco.

regions.name: Marche
regions.summary: Adriatic hills: crisp Verdicchio and Montepulciano-based Rosso Conero.

regions.name: Abruzzo
regions.summary: Mountains and sea: soft, plummy Montepulciano d'Abruzzo and Cerasuolo rosé.

regions.name: Campania
regions.summary: Volcanic soils around Vesuvius and Avellino: Taurasi (Aglianico), Fiano di Avellino and Greco di Tufo.

regions.name: Puglia
regions.summary: The hot, flat heel of Italy: ripe Primitivo and Negroamaro.

regions.name: Basilicata
regions.summary: Aglianico del Vulture, grown on the slopes of an extinct volcano.

regions.name: Sicily
regions.summary: Sunny island making ripe Nero d'Avola, elegant wines from the volcanic slopes of Mount Etna, and fortified Marsala.

regions.name: Sardinia
regions.summary: Island of Cannonau (Grenache) and Vermentino di Gallura.

regions.name: Spain
regions.climate: Mostly hot and dry; the central plateau (Meseta) is high and continental; green, rainy Atlantic north-west.
regions.summary: The country with the most vineyard area in the world: Rioja and Ribera del Duero reds, Cava, Albariño and the unique fortified Sherry.
regions.classification: DOCa/DOQ (Rioja, Priorat) → DO → Vino de la Tierra. Age terms: **Joven**, **Crianza**, **Reserva**, **Gran Reserva** (longer ageing in oak and bottle).
regions.history: Phoenicians and Romans planted Spain's first vineyards; the Moors limited wine but kept vines for table grapes. Sherry traded with England for centuries, and phylloxera in France sent French merchants to Rioja in the 1870s. After Franco, Spain modernized fast: Ribera del Duero, Priorat and Rías Baixas rose from almost nothing in the 1980s–90s.

regions.name: Rioja
regions.climate: Continental, protected by mountains from Atlantic weather; cooler in the west (Rioja Alta, Alavesa), warmer in the east (Rioja Oriental).
regions.summary: Spain's classic: Tempranillo-led blends, traditionally aged in American oak for vanilla and coconut notes.
regions.classification: Crianza (2 years, 1 in oak), Reserva (3 years, 1 in oak), Gran Reserva (5 years, 2 in oak).
regions.history: When phylloxera and mildew hit Bordeaux in the 1860s–70s, French merchants came to Rioja for wine, bringing oak barrels and Bordeaux methods. A railway from Haro took the wine north. Houses founded then, such as López de Heredia (1877) and CVNE (1879), still define classic, long-aged Rioja.

regions.name: Ribera del Duero
regions.climate: High altitude (750–850 m) with hot days and very cold nights.
regions.summary: Powerful, dark Tempranillo (Tinto Fino) along the Duero river. Vega Sicilia is the legend.
regions.history: Vega Sicilia, founded in 1864 with Bordeaux vines, was for a century Spain's only famous red from the Duero. When Alejandro Fernández's Pesquera won praise from Robert Parker in the 1980s, the region boomed and gained its DO in 1982.

regions.name: Priorat
regions.summary: Steep slopes of llicorella slate: intense, mineral Garnacha and Cariñena from old, low-yielding vines.

regions.name: Rías Baixas
regions.climate: Cool, wet, Atlantic; vines trained high on pergolas for airflow.
regions.summary: Galicia's green coast: fresh, saline Albariño.

regions.name: Rueda
regions.summary: High plateau whites from Verdejo: fresh, herbal and citrusy.

regions.name: Toro
regions.summary: Hot and dry: powerful, ripe Tinta de Toro (Tempranillo).

regions.name: Bierzo
regions.summary: Fragrant Mencía from slate slopes in Castilla y León's green north-west.

regions.name: Navarra
regions.summary: Rioja's neighbor, known for Garnacha rosado and modern reds.

regions.name: Penedès
regions.summary: Near Barcelona: the heart of Cava, Spain's traditional-method sparkling wine.

regions.name: La Mancha
regions.summary: Vast, hot, flat plateau: Spain's largest DO, for value wines (Airén, Tempranillo).

regions.name: Jumilla
regions.summary: Hot inland south-east: ripe, dark Monastrell.

regions.name: Jerez (Sherry)
regions.climate: Hot, with cooling, humid Atlantic winds (poniente) that favor flor; white albariza chalk soils retain water.
regions.summary: The Sherry Triangle of Jerez, El Puerto de Santa María and Sanlúcar de Barrameda: fortified wines aged in solera systems.

regions.name: Portugal
regions.climate: Atlantic-influenced and wet in the north-west, hot and dry inland and in the south.
regions.summary: A treasure trove of native grapes: Port and Madeira, fresh Vinho Verde and increasingly world-class dry reds from the Douro, Dão and Alentejo.
regions.classification: DOC (Denominação de Origem Controlada) → Vinho Regional.
regions.history: Portugal's long alliance with England shaped its wine. The Methuen Treaty of 1703 gave Portuguese wine low taxes in England, and fortified Douro wine became Port. Madeira, heated on long voyages, became America's favorite wine in colonial times; toasts at the signing of the Declaration of Independence were made with it.

regions.name: Vinho Verde
regions.climate: Cool, rainy and green.
regions.summary: Light, zesty, sometimes slightly spritzy whites; Alvarinho from Monção e Melgaço is the finest.

regions.name: Douro
regions.climate: Hot, dry continental, sheltered by mountains; vineyards on steep schist terraces.
regions.summary: The dramatic terraced valley of Port, now also famous for powerful dry reds. The world's first demarcated wine region (1756).
regions.history: The Marquis of Pombal demarcated the Douro in 1756, one of the first protected wine regions. Terraces were cut by hand into schist over centuries. British families such as Taylor's, Croft and Graham's built lodges in Vila Nova de Gaia, where Port aged before shipping. UNESCO listed the valley in 2001.

regions.name: Dão
regions.summary: Granite plateau ringed by mountains: elegant reds and Encruzado whites.

regions.name: Bairrada
regions.summary: Near the coast: tannic Baga reds and traditional-method sparkling wines.

regions.name: Lisboa
regions.summary: Atlantic-cooled region north of Lisbon producing fresh, good-value blends.

regions.name: Tejo
regions.summary: Fertile Tagus river plains making easy-drinking reds and whites.

regions.name: Setúbal
regions.summary: Peninsula south of Lisbon, famous for fortified Moscatel de Setúbal.

regions.name: Alentejo
regions.summary: Hot, rolling plains (and cork forests): ripe, generous reds. Some wines still made in clay talhas.

regions.name: Germany
regions.climate: Cool continental; the best vineyards are steep, south-facing river slopes that catch the sun and reflected heat.
regions.summary: Riesling's homeland: racy, aromatic whites from bone dry to lusciously sweet, along the Rhine, Mosel and their tributaries. Spätburgunder (Pinot Noir) is increasingly fine.
regions.classification: Prädikatswein ripeness levels by sugar at harvest: **Kabinett**, **Spätlese**, **Auslese**, **Beerenauslese**, **Eiswein**, **Trockenbeerenauslese**. Trocken means dry. VDP estates use Grosse Lage/Grosses Gewächs for top dry wines.
regions.history: The Romans planted the Mosel and the monks of Kloster Eberbach made the Rheingau famous. In 1775 a late messenger at Schloss Johannisberg delayed the harvest and gave birth to Spätlese. In the 1800s top Rieslings cost more than Bordeaux First Growths; two wars and cheap sweet exports damaged its name, now rebuilt by dry Grosses Gewächs wines.

regions.name: Mosel
regions.climate: Very cool; steep blue slate slopes above the winding river absorb and reflect heat.
regions.summary: The world's steepest vineyards: delicate, low-alcohol Riesling with high acidity, often off-dry or sweet.
regions.history: Roman poet Ausonius praised the Mosel's vineyards in the 4th century. Monks and electors planted Riesling on the steep slate slopes from the 1400s. The light, slightly sweet Kabinett style made it famous; today warmer summers let growers make more dry Riesling too.

regions.name: Rheingau
regions.summary: Where the Rhine flows west, giving a long south-facing slope: fuller, often drier Riesling. Schloss Johannisberg discovered late harvest in 1775.

regions.name: Rheinhessen
regions.summary: Germany's largest region, once known for bulk Liebfraumilch, now for a new generation of dry wines.

regions.name: Pfalz
regions.summary: Warm and sunny below the Haardt mountains: ripe, full dry Riesling and Pinots.

regions.name: Nahe
regions.summary: Varied volcanic and slate soils: precise, mineral Riesling.

regions.name: Ahr
regions.summary: A small northern valley famous for red Spätburgunder.

regions.name: Mittelrhein
regions.summary: The romantic castle-lined gorge of the Rhine: steep slate Riesling.

regions.name: Franken
regions.summary: Dry, earthy Silvaner in the flat, round Bocksbeutel bottle.

regions.name: Baden
regions.summary: Germany's warmest, southernmost region: Pinot Noir, Grauburgunder and Weissburgunder.

regions.name: Württemberg
regions.summary: Red-wine country around Stuttgart: Trollinger and Lemberger.

regions.name: Saale-Unstrut
regions.summary: One of Europe's most northerly quality regions, in former East Germany.

regions.name: Sachsen
regions.summary: Tiny region around Dresden along the Elbe.

regions.name: Austria
regions.climate: Continental: warm days and cool nights; the Danube and Lake Neusiedl moderate temperatures.
regions.summary: Precise, dry whites led by Grüner Veltliner and Riesling, serious reds from Burgenland and world-class sweet wines around Lake Neusiedl.
regions.classification: DAC (Districtus Austriae Controllatus) marks typical regional styles. In the Wachau: Steinfeder, Federspiel and Smaragd by ripeness.
regions.history: Vines have grown along the Danube since the Celts and Romans. In 1985 a few brokers were caught sweetening wine with glycol, and exports collapsed. Austria answered with some of the strictest wine laws in Europe and rebuilt its name on dry Grüner Veltliner and Riesling from the Wachau, Kamptal and Kremstal.

regions.name: Wachau
regions.climate: Cool, but warm air from the Pannonian plain and the Danube help ripen grapes on steep terraces.
regions.summary: Steep stone terraces above the Danube: Austria's most famous dry Riesling and Grüner Veltliner (Smaragd is the ripest category).

regions.name: Kremstal
regions.summary: Around the town of Krems, next to the Wachau: Grüner and Riesling on loess and rock.

regions.name: Kamptal
regions.summary: Along the Kamp river; the Heiligenstein vineyard is famous for Riesling.

regions.name: Wagram
regions.summary: Deep loess terraces, rich Grüner Veltliner and Roter Veltliner.

regions.name: Weinviertel
regions.summary: Austria's largest region, the 'wine quarter': peppery Grüner Veltliner.

regions.name: Carnuntum
regions.summary: Roman-era region east of Vienna making juicy reds.

regions.name: Thermenregion
regions.summary: Spa-town region south of Vienna with local whites and Pinot Noir.

regions.name: Neusiedlersee
regions.climate: The shallow lake creates humid mists that encourage noble rot.
regions.summary: Around Lake Neusiedl: juicy Zweigelt and world-class botrytized sweet wines (Ausbruch, TBA).

regions.name: Leithaberg
regions.summary: Limestone and schist hills west of the lake: mineral Blaufränkisch and Chardonnay.

regions.name: Mittelburgenland
regions.summary: 'Blaufränkischland': structured, peppery Blaufränkisch.

regions.name: Steiermark (Styria)
regions.summary: Steep green hills in the south: vibrant Sauvignon Blanc and Morillon (Chardonnay).

regions.name: Hungary
regions.climate: Continental, with hot summers and long autumns.
regions.summary: Home of Tokaji, the 'wine of kings, king of wines', plus red Bull's Blood (Egri Bikavér) and wines from around Lake Balaton.
regions.history: Hungary's wine culture flourished under the Habsburgs. Tokaj was classified in 1730 and was the toast of European courts. Communism (1949–1989) turned vineyards into state farms; since the 1990s private and foreign investment has revived Tokaj and red regions such as Villány and Eger.

regions.name: Tokaj
regions.climate: Autumn mists from the Bodrog and Tisza rivers encourage noble rot.
regions.summary: Volcanic hills producing Tokaji Aszú, made by adding botrytized aszú berries to a base wine, plus dry Furmint and the rare Eszencia.
facts: Tokaj's vineyards were classified in the 1730s, over a century before Bordeaux's 1855 classification.
regions.history: Noble-rot wines were made in Tokaj by the 1600s; by legend a harvest delayed by a Turkish raid revealed the magic of botrytis. The vineyards were classified in 1730, and Louis XIV called Tokaji 'the wine of kings, the king of wines'. After decades as a state farm, the region was revived from 1990 by Royal Tokaji and others.

regions.name: Eger
regions.summary: Known for Egri Bikavér, 'Bull's Blood', a Kékfrankos-based red blend.

regions.name: Villány
regions.summary: Hungary's warm south: ripe Bordeaux-style reds.

regions.name: Szekszárd
regions.summary: Loess hills making Bikavér-style blends and Kadarka.

regions.name: Balaton
regions.summary: Volcanic hills around Central Europe's largest lake: aromatic whites.

regions.name: Somló
regions.summary: A single extinct volcano with intense, smoky whites.

regions.name: Kunság
regions.summary: Great Plain sands: Hungary's largest region for everyday wines.

regions.name: Greece
regions.climate: Mediterranean, moderated by altitude, sea breezes and the summer Meltemi wind.
regions.summary: One of the oldest wine cultures on earth, with over 300 native grapes and a modern revival led by Assyrtiko, Xinomavro and Agiorgitiko.
regions.history: Ancient Greece built a wine culture, with festivals for Dionysus, symposia and amphorae shipped around the Mediterranean. Centuries of Ottoman rule and then war held winemaking back. Since the 1980s a new generation has rediscovered native grapes such as Assyrtiko, Xinomavro and Agiorgitiko.

regions.name: Santorini
regions.summary: Volcanic island of mineral Assyrtiko from ancient, ungrafted basket-trained vines; also sweet Vinsanto.
regions.history: On this volcanic island, vines grow in sand-like ash that phylloxera cannot cross, so some roots are centuries old. Growers weave vines into low baskets, kouloura, to protect grapes from wind. Its Vinsanto, a sweet wine from sun-dried grapes, was traded across the Mediterranean in Venetian times.

regions.name: Naoussa
regions.summary: Macedonian slopes producing structured, age-worthy Xinomavro.

regions.name: Amyndeo
regions.summary: Cool, high-altitude region known for Xinomavro rosé and sparkling.

regions.name: Nemea
regions.summary: Peloponnese home of Agiorgitiko.

regions.name: Mantinia
regions.summary: High plateau whites from aromatic Moschofilero.

regions.name: Patras
regions.summary: Known for sweet Muscat and Mavrodaphne.

regions.name: Crete
regions.summary: Greece's largest island, with native grapes like Vidiano and Liatiko.

regions.name: United States
regions.climate: California: Mediterranean, cooled by Pacific fog and breezes. Oregon: cool and wet. Eastern Washington: hot, dry desert irrigated by rivers.
regions.summary: Wine is made in all 50 states, but the West Coast leads: Napa Cabernet, Sonoma Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, Oregon Pinot and Washington's Bordeaux varieties.
regions.classification: Wines are labeled by grape. AVAs (American Viticultural Areas) define places; a varietal wine must contain at least 75% of the named grape.
regions.history: Spanish missionaries planted vines in California from 1769. The Gold Rush brought immigrants, and Napa and Sonoma grew quickly until phylloxera and then Prohibition (1920–1933) closed most wineries. Robert Mondavi's winery (1966) and the 1976 Judgment of Paris began the modern era.

regions.name: Napa & Sonoma
regions.climate: Warm, sunny days; cool fog and wind from the Pacific and San Pablo Bay in the south and west.
regions.summary: California's North Coast: Napa Valley for world-famous Cabernet; larger, more varied Sonoma for Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Zinfandel.
facts: At the 1976 'Judgment of Paris', Napa wines beat top Bordeaux and Burgundy in a blind tasting.

regions.name: Napa Valley
regions.climate: Cooler in the south near the bay, hotter up-valley toward Calistoga.
regions.summary: America's most famous wine region: ripe, plush, oak-aged Cabernet Sauvignon and blends.
regions.history: Charles Krug founded Napa's first commercial winery in 1861. Prohibition shut most of the valley; Beaulieu Vineyard kept going with sacramental wine. Robert Mondavi's Oakville winery (1966) and Stag's Leap's victory at the 1976 Judgment of Paris made Napa Cabernet world-famous.

regions.name: Oakville
regions.summary: The heart of the valley floor: benchmark Napa Cabernet (To Kalon vineyard).

regions.name: Rutherford
regions.summary: Known for 'Rutherford dust', a dusty, cocoa-like texture in its Cabernet.

regions.name: Stags Leap District
regions.summary: Silky, perfumed Cabernet from the east side; won the 1976 Judgment of Paris.

regions.name: Howell Mountain
regions.summary: Above the fog line: powerful, tannic mountain Cabernet.

regions.name: Mount Veeder
regions.summary: Steep western hills: firm, structured mountain wines.

regions.name: Los Carneros
regions.climate: Cool and windy, at the edge of San Pablo Bay.
regions.summary: Straddles Napa and Sonoma: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and sparkling wine.

regions.name: Sonoma Coast
regions.summary: Cool, foggy coastal ridges: taut, elegant Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

regions.name: Russian River Valley
regions.summary: Morning fog funnels up the river: ripe yet fresh Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

regions.name: Sonoma Valley
regions.summary: The 'Valley of the Moon': historic estates and varied wines.

regions.name: Dry Creek Valley
regions.summary: Benchmark old-vine Zinfandel near Healdsburg.

regions.name: Alexander Valley
regions.summary: Warm inland Sonoma valley: soft, generous Cabernet.

regions.name: Central Coast
regions.summary: From Santa Cruz to Santa Barbara: cool valleys open to the ocean (Santa Rita Hills) for Pinot and Chardonnay; warmer Paso Robles for Rhône and Bordeaux varieties.

regions.name: Lodi
regions.summary: Inland, warm, with Delta breezes: famous for old-vine Zinfandel.

regions.name: Mendocino
regions.summary: Rugged north coast; Anderson Valley is known for Pinot Noir and sparkling wine.

regions.name: Sierra Foothills
regions.summary: Gold Rush country with gnarled old Zinfandel vines.

regions.name: Central Valley
regions.summary: Hot and vast: the source of most inexpensive California wine.

regions.name: Willamette Valley
regions.climate: Cool and wet, sheltered by the Coast Range.
regions.summary: Oregon's heart: elegant, Burgundian Pinot Noir and Pinot Gris.

regions.name: Southern Oregon
regions.summary: Warmer valleys (Umpqua, Rogue) growing a wide range of grapes.

regions.name: Columbia Valley
regions.climate: Semi-desert east of the Cascades: hot days, cold nights, irrigation from the Columbia river.
regions.summary: Washington's vast region: ripe, fresh Cabernet, Merlot, Syrah and Riesling.

regions.name: Walla Walla
regions.summary: Famous for savory Syrah grown on cobblestones (The Rocks District).

regions.name: Chile
regions.climate: Mediterranean. The cold Humboldt Current cools the coast; the Andes send cold air down at night.
regions.summary: A long, thin country between the Andes and the Pacific. Reliable sunshine gives ripe, fruity Cabernet and Carmenère; cool coastal valleys make crisp whites and Pinot.
facts: Chile has never been hit by phylloxera, thanks to natural barriers: desert, mountains, ocean and ice.
Regions are now also labeled Costa (coastal), Entre Cordilleras (between the ranges) and Andes.
regions.history: Spanish conquistadors and missionaries planted País vines in the 1550s. In the 1850s landowners imported Bordeaux vines, including Carmenère, just before phylloxera struck France. Protected by mountains, ocean and desert, Chile never had phylloxera; Carmenère was rediscovered there in 1994, long mistaken for Merlot.

regions.name: Maipo Valley
regions.summary: Around Santiago: Chile's classic Cabernet Sauvignon, often with a minty edge in Alto Maipo.

regions.name: Colchagua
regions.summary: Warm valley famous for rich reds, especially Carmenère.

regions.name: Casablanca Valley
regions.climate: Cool, with morning fog from the Pacific.
regions.summary: Chile's original cool-climate region, between Santiago and the coast: crisp whites and Pinot Noir.

regions.name: Aconcagua
regions.summary: Named after the Americas' highest peak: warm-valley reds and cool coastal whites.

regions.name: Maule
regions.summary: Large southern region with old, dry-farmed bush vines of Carignan and País.

regions.name: Itata & Bío Bío
regions.summary: Cool, rainy south: old-vine Cinsault and País, plus aromatic whites.

regions.name: Elqui & Limarí
regions.summary: Desert north: limestone-rich Limarí makes mineral Chardonnay.

regions.name: Argentina
regions.climate: High-altitude desert at the foot of the Andes: intense sun, big day–night temperature swings, irrigation from snowmelt.
regions.summary: The world's Malbec capital. Altitude is everything: vineyards lie from about 600 m to over 3,000 m above sea level.
regions.history: Missionaries brought vines in the 1550s; Italian and Spanish immigrants in the late 1800s built a huge industry for home drinking. In the 1990s producers such as Nicolás Catena bet on quality and exports, and Malbec from high Mendoza vineyards became Argentina's signature.

regions.name: Mendoza
regions.summary: About 70% of Argentina's wine: ripe, velvety Malbec from Luján de Cuyo and Maipú.
regions.history: Irrigation canals first dug by the Huarpe people, then extended by Spanish settlers, turned Mendoza's desert into vineyards fed by Andean snowmelt. A railway from Buenos Aires (1885) opened its market. From the 1990s, altitude vineyards in the Uco Valley made it a world name for Malbec.

regions.name: Uco Valley
regions.climate: High (900–1,500 m) and cool at night.
regions.summary: Mendoza's high-altitude star: fresher, more floral Malbec and fine Chardonnay.

regions.name: Salta
regions.summary: Some of the highest vineyards in the world around Cafayate: aromatic Torrontés and intense reds.

regions.name: San Juan
regions.summary: Hot region north of Mendoza, known for Syrah.

regions.name: Patagonia
regions.summary: Cooler, windy south (Neuquén, Río Negro): Pinot Noir and fresh Malbec.

regions.name: Australia
regions.climate: Mostly warm to hot; quality regions are in the cooler south, near the coast or at altitude.
regions.summary: Bold, fruit-driven Shiraz made Australia famous, but its cool regions now shine for Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Riesling.
regions.classification: Labeled by grape; Geographical Indications (GIs) define zones, regions and subregions.
facts: Some of the world's oldest vines, ungrafted Shiraz and Grenache from the 1840s, still grow in the Barossa.
South Australia has never had phylloxera.
regions.history: Vines arrived with the First Fleet in 1788. James Busby brought hundreds of cuttings from Europe in the 1830s, and German Lutherans settled the Barossa in the 1840s. Strict quarantine kept phylloxera out of South Australia, so some of the world's oldest vines grow there. Penfolds Grange (1951) proved Australia could make icons.

regions.name: Barossa Valley
regions.climate: Warm and dry.
regions.summary: Australia's most famous region: rich, ripe Shiraz with chocolate and spice, from some of the world's oldest vines.
regions.history: Silesian Lutherans fleeing persecution settled the valley from 1842 and planted Shiraz, Grenache and Mourvèdre. Phylloxera never reached South Australia, so vines from the 1840s still produce wine. In the 1980s, growers were paid to pull out old vines; champions such as Peter Lehmann saved many of them.

regions.name: Eden Valley
regions.summary: Higher and cooler hills beside the Barossa: lime-scented Riesling and elegant Shiraz.

regions.name: Clare Valley
regions.climate: Warm days and cool nights.
regions.summary: Famous for bone-dry, lime-scented Riesling that ages to toast.

regions.name: McLaren Vale
regions.climate: Mediterranean, cooled by the sea.
regions.summary: Coastal warmth: generous Shiraz and Grenache.

regions.name: Adelaide Hills
regions.summary: Cool, high hills: fresh Sauvignon Blanc and fine Chardonnay.

regions.name: Coonawarra
regions.climate: Cool, with sea breezes.
regions.summary: A strip of red 'terra rossa' soil over limestone: Australia's classic Cabernet, often with mint.

regions.name: Langhorne Creek
regions.summary: Lake-cooled region making soft, approachable reds.

regions.name: Padthaway
regions.summary: Limestone Coast region north of Coonawarra.

regions.name: Riverland
regions.summary: Hot, irrigated Murray river region producing large volumes of value wine.

regions.name: Margaret River
regions.climate: Maritime, almost surrounded by ocean.
regions.summary: Western Australia's star: elegant Cabernet and Chardonnay, and crisp Sémillon–Sauvignon blends.

regions.name: Great Southern
regions.summary: Vast, cool region in WA: Riesling and peppery Shiraz.

regions.name: Swan Valley
regions.summary: Hot, historic region near Perth.

regions.name: Yarra Valley
regions.climate: Cool, near Melbourne.
regions.summary: Elegant Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and sparkling wine.

regions.name: Rutherglen
regions.summary: Hot north-east Victoria: famous for luscious fortified Rutherglen Muscat.

regions.name: Riverina
regions.summary: Hot, irrigated region; known for big volumes and botrytized Sémillon.

regions.name: Hunter Valley
regions.climate: Hot, humid, with afternoon cloud and summer rain.
regions.summary: Unique, long-lived Hunter Sémillon (low alcohol, ages to toast and honey) and medium-bodied Shiraz.

regions.name: Tasmania
regions.climate: Cool maritime.
regions.summary: Australia's coolest state: superb sparkling wine, Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

regions.name: New Zealand
regions.climate: Cool maritime: no vineyard is more than about 130 km from the sea. Long, sunny days with cool nights.
regions.summary: Intense, pure-fruited wines. Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc became a global style; Central Otago and Martinborough make fine Pinot Noir.
regions.history: Missionary Samuel Marsden planted New Zealand's first vines in 1819. For a century the industry was small and focused on fortified wine. Marlborough's first commercial vineyards were planted in 1973, and Cloudy Bay's 1985 Sauvignon Blanc made the country famous almost overnight.

regions.name: Marlborough
regions.climate: Sunny and dry with cold nights, ideal for aromatic intensity and high acidity.
regions.summary: New Zealand's largest region: pungent Sauvignon Blanc with passion fruit, gooseberry and grassy notes.
regions.history: Marlborough was sheep country until Montana planted vines in 1973. Sunny days, cold nights and stony soils gave Sauvignon Blanc an intense, pungent style unlike any other. Cloudy Bay's 1985 release launched a worldwide category; today the region makes most of New Zealand's wine.

regions.name: Central Otago
regions.climate: The world's most southerly major region; continental, with hot days and cold nights.
regions.summary: Dramatic mountain region making ripe, intense, dark-cherry Pinot Noir.

regions.name: Hawke's Bay
regions.summary: Warmer North Island region: Bordeaux blends and peppery Syrah from the Gimblett Gravels.

regions.name: Martinborough
regions.summary: Small Wairarapa village known for savory, structured Pinot Noir.

regions.name: Nelson
regions.summary: Sunny, artsy region next to Marlborough.

regions.name: North Canterbury
regions.summary: Limestone-rich Waipara Valley: Riesling and Pinot Noir.

regions.name: Gisborne
regions.summary: The first vineyards to see the sunrise; known for Chardonnay.

regions.name: Auckland & Waiheke
regions.summary: Warm Waiheke Island makes Bordeaux blends and Syrah.

regions.name: South Africa
regions.climate: Mediterranean, cooled by the cold Benguela Current and the strong south-easterly wind, the 'Cape Doctor'.
regions.summary: Wine since 1659, with Old World restraint and New World fruit. The world's largest Chenin Blanc plantings and the home of Pinotage.
regions.classification: Wine of Origin (WO) scheme: regions, districts and wards.
regions.history: The Dutch East India Company planted vines at the Cape in 1655, and Constantia's sweet wine was drunk by Napoleon and Jane Austen's heroines. Phylloxera, then the KWV cooperative's focus on volume, and sanctions under apartheid held the Cape back; since 1994 it has reinvented itself around old-vine Chenin Blanc and regions such as Swartland.

regions.name: Stellenbosch
regions.summary: The Cape's most famous district: mountainous, varied sites for Cabernet, Bordeaux blends and Pinotage.

regions.name: Swartland
regions.climate: Hot and dry; old, dry-farmed bush vines.
regions.summary: The 'Swartland revolution': characterful old-vine Chenin and Rhône-style blends.

regions.name: Paarl
regions.summary: Warm inland district beneath a granite outcrop.

regions.name: Franschhoek
regions.summary: 'French corner', settled by Huguenots: old Sémillon and Cap Classique sparkling wine.

regions.name: Constantia
regions.summary: Historic cool slopes near Cape Town: Sauvignon Blanc and the legendary sweet Vin de Constance, loved by Napoleon.

regions.name: Elgin
regions.summary: Cool, high apple country: crisp whites and Pinot Noir.

regions.name: Walker Bay
regions.summary: Hemel-en-Aarde ('heaven and earth') near Hermanus: Burgundian Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

regions.name: Durbanville
regions.summary: Breezy hills near Cape Town: zesty Sauvignon Blanc.

regions.name: Robertson
regions.summary: Limestone soils inland: Chardonnay and sparkling wine.

regions.name: Breedekloof
regions.summary: Large valley region known for value Chenin Blanc.

regions.name: Tulbagh
regions.summary: Mountain-ringed valley with Rhône varieties and sparkling wine.

regions.name: Cape Agulhas (Elim)
regions.summary: Africa's southernmost vineyards: cool, windswept Sauvignon Blanc.

regions.name: Lebanon
regions.climate: Mediterranean, but the vineyards sit high: the Bekaa Valley floor is around 1,000 m, giving hot days, cold nights and a long, dry growing season.
regions.summary: One of the oldest wine cultures on earth, from Phoenician traders to the Temple of Bacchus at Baalbek. Today it is known for structured red blends from the high Bekaa Valley.
regions.classification: No formal appellation system yet; wines are labeled by producer, region and grape.
regions.styles: Bordeaux- and Rhône-style red blends, often Cabernet Sauvignon with Cinsault, Carignan or Syrah; fresh whites from native Obaideh and Merwah; dry rosé from Cinsault.
facts: **Château Musar** (founded 1930) made Lebanon famous, with long-lived reds released years after the vintage.
**Château Ksara**, founded by Jesuits in 1857, keeps its wine in Roman-era limestone caves.
Most vineyards lie in the **Bekaa Valley**, a high plateau between the Mount Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon ranges.
**Obaideh** and **Merwah** are native white grapes, sometimes compared to Chardonnay and Sémillon.
regions.history: Phoenician traders from the Lebanese coast spread wine across the Mediterranean 3,000 years ago, and the Romans built the Temple of Bacchus at Baalbek. Jesuit monks founded Château Ksara in 1857 with French vines. Château Musar kept making wine through the civil war (1975–1990), and since then dozens of new estates have opened.

regions.name: Bekaa Valley
regions.climate: High plateau (about 1,000 m): sunny, dry summers with cool nights.
regions.summary: The heart of Lebanese wine, from Zahlé south to the West Bekaa (Kefraya, Ammiq): home to Ksara and many leading estates. Ripe, spicy red blends with fresh acidity from the altitude.
regions.history: The high plateau between the Mount Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon ranges has grown grapes since antiquity. Jesuits planted Cinsault and Bordeaux varieties at Ksara in 1857; Château Kefraya and Château Musar's vineyards followed. Today most Lebanese wine comes from the Bekaa, at about 1,000 m.

regions.name: Baalbek
regions.summary: The northern Bekaa, near the Roman Temple of Bacchus. Drier and higher, with old bush vines and a growing number of new estates.

regions.name: Mount Lebanon
regions.summary: Terraced mountain vineyards above Beirut and Byblos, south to the green hills of Jezzine; Château Musar's winery is in Ghazir. Fresh whites and lighter reds.

regions.name: Batroun
regions.summary: Coastal hills in the north with a cluster of small family wineries; sea breezes and limestone soils.

aromas.name: Primary
aromas.summary: Aromas from the **grape** and alcoholic fermentation: fruit, flowers, herbs and spice. They dominate young wines.

categories.name: Floral
categories.note: Floral notes lift aromatic grapes such as Muscat, Gewürztraminer, Riesling and Viognier, and violet is classic in Malbec and Syrah.

categories.name: Green fruit
categories.note: Typical of cool-climate whites: crisp, tart and fresh.

categories.name: Citrus
categories.note: High-acid whites from cool to moderate climates.

categories.name: Stone fruit
categories.note: Riper whites from moderate climates: Viognier, Albariño, riper Chardonnay.

categories.name: Tropical
categories.note: Warm-climate ripeness, or certain aromatic grapes and cool fermentations.

categories.name: Red fruit
categories.note: Lighter reds and cooler climates: Pinot Noir, Gamay, Grenache, Sangiovese.

categories.name: Black fruit
categories.note: Fuller reds from moderate to warm climates: Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Malbec.

categories.name: Dried fruit
categories.note: Very ripe grapes from hot climates, dried grapes (Amarone, PX) or age.

categories.name: Herbaceous
categories.note: Green, leafy notes from compounds called methoxypyrazines, common in Sauvignon Blanc, Cabernets and Carmenère, especially when less ripe.

categories.name: Herbal
categories.note: Dried and fresh herbs: classic in southern French and Mediterranean reds (garrigue) and Australian Cabernet (eucalyptus, mint).

categories.name: Spice
categories.note: Peppery notes from the grape itself, most famously in cool-climate Syrah and Grüner Veltliner.

categories.name: Mineral
categories.note: Hard-to-pin notes often linked to cool climates, high acidity or reductive winemaking.

aromas.name: Secondary
aromas.summary: Aromas from **winemaking** after fermentation: yeast lees, malolactic conversion and oak.

categories.name: Lees
categories.note: From contact with dead yeast cells (lees), as in Champagne and lees-aged Muscadet.

categories.name: Malolactic
categories.note: Malolactic conversion turns tart malic acid into softer lactic acid, often adding buttery, creamy notes (diacetyl).

categories.name: Oak
categories.note: New oak barrels, especially toasted ones, add sweet spice and smoky notes. American oak is more coconut and vanilla; French oak is subtler and spicier.

aromas.name: Tertiary
aromas.summary: Aromas from **ageing**, in barrel or bottle. Fresh fruit fades into dried fruit, and savory, earthy notes develop.

categories.name: Aged red
categories.note: Bottle-aged reds develop savory, earthy complexity.

categories.name: Aged white
categories.note: Aged whites gain honeyed, nutty and dried-fruit notes. Petrol is a famous sign of aged Riesling.

categories.name: Oxidative
categories.note: Deliberate exposure to oxygen during long ageing, as in Tawny Port, Oloroso Sherry and Madeira.

colors.name: Lemon-green
colors.note: Pale with a green tinge. Very young, unoaked, cool-climate whites such as Muscadet, young Riesling or Grüner Veltliner.

colors.name: Lemon
colors.note: The most common white color. Most young dry whites, from Sauvignon Blanc to Pinot Grigio.

colors.name: Gold
colors.note: Richer and deeper. Oak-aged or older whites, warm-climate Chardonnay and sweet wines such as Sauternes.

colors.name: Amber
colors.note: Long ageing or deliberate oxidation: old sweet wines, Tokaji, tawny-style fortified wines and orange wines.

colors.name: Brown
colors.note: Very old or heavily oxidized wine, such as old Oloroso or Pedro Ximénez Sherry. In a table wine, a sign it is past its best.

colors.name: Pink
colors.note: Bright, youthful rosé. Often from Grenache, Pinot Noir or Sangiovese with very short skin contact.

colors.name: Salmon
colors.note: Pale pink-orange, the classic Provence look. Delicate, dry and fashionable.

colors.name: Orange
colors.note: Deeper orange tones, from oak, age or certain grapes. Some traditional rosados and older rosés.

colors.name: Purple
colors.note: Very young red with a vivid violet rim. Young Syrah, Malbec, Beaujolais or barrel samples.

colors.name: Ruby
colors.note: The typical young red: bright red core. Most reds in their first few years.

colors.name: Garnet
colors.note: Red with an orange-brick rim. Older reds, or naturally pale, quick-to-age grapes such as Nebbiolo and Pinot Noir.

colors.name: Tawny
colors.note: Brownish orange. Long barrel-aged wines such as Tawny Port, or reds of considerable age.

glossary.def: The tart, mouthwatering quality of wine. It keeps wine fresh and helps it age.
The percentage of alcohol in a wine, usually 11–15% for table wines.
A smell from the grape or fermentation; often used for any smell in wine.
The sense of weight and richness in the mouth, from light to full.
A wine with little or no perceptible sugar.
How long the flavors linger after swallowing; a long finish is a sign of quality.
Wine with added grape spirit, such as Port or Sherry.
Pink wine made from black grapes with brief skin contact.
Wine with dissolved carbon dioxide bubbles.
Wine without bubbles.
Compounds from skins, seeds, stems and oak that dry and grip the gums.
A type of grape, such as Merlot or Chardonnay.
The year the grapes were harvested.
Yeast converting sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide.
A wine tainted by TCA, smelling of damp cardboard or wet dog, with muted fruit.
A wine spoiled by too much oxygen: dull, brownish, with bruised-apple notes.
Pouring wine into another vessel to separate it from sediment or let it breathe.
Solid deposits that form in some wines, especially older reds and Vintage Port.
Slightly sweet.
A wine named after (and made mainly from) one grape variety.
Wine made from more than one grape variety, vineyard or vintage.
The traditional wine countries of Europe and the Mediterranean.
Wine countries outside Europe, such as the USA, Australia, Chile and New Zealand.
The smell of a wine, or the act of smelling it.
The taste and texture of a wine in the mouth.
A savory taste found in mushrooms, cured meats, aged cheese and soy sauce.
A legally defined wine region with rules on grapes and winemaking.
France's protected designation of origin: the highest category of French wine.
Italy's highest quality category, Denominazione di Origine Controllata e Garantita.
Protected Designation of Origin: the EU's strictest category for regional wines.
Protected Geographical Indication: a broader EU regional category with more flexible rules (IGP, IGT, Vino de la Tierra).
The whole natural environment of a vineyard (soil, slope, aspect, climate) and how it shapes the wine.
The average weather pattern of a region over many years.
Year-to-year conditions that create vintage variation.
Large differences between hot summers and cold winters, far from the sea.
Small temperature differences between seasons, moderated by the sea, often with rain.
Long, warm, dry summers and mild winters.
When the first green shoots emerge from the buds in spring.
When the vine's tiny flowers open and are pollinated, in late spring.
When pollinated flowers become tiny berries.
When grapes soften and change color, marking the start of ripening.
Picking the grapes, by hand or machine.
The vine's winter rest.
Freshly pressed grape juice, with or without skins, before or during fermentation.
Dead yeast cells that settle after fermentation. Contact adds texture and bready flavors.
Aged on the lees, as in Muscadet sur lie.
Bacteria turning tart malic acid into softer lactic acid, often adding a buttery note.
Soaking grape skins in the juice or wine to extract color, tannin and flavor.
The layer of skins that floats to the top during red fermentation.
Pushing the cap of skins back into the fermenting wine.
Pumping wine from the bottom of the tank over the cap.
Adding sugar to the must to increase final alcohol; allowed in some cool regions.
Adding acid to the must in hot regions where grapes lack it.
Adding an agent (bentonite, egg white) to remove haze-causing particles.
Passing wine through a filter to remove particles and microbes.
A 225-liter oak barrel, the Bordeaux standard.
Stirring the lees in a barrel to add creamy texture.
Fermenting whole uncrushed bunches in CO₂, giving soft, fruity, bubblegum-scented reds.
Fermenting grapes with stems attached, for fragrance and structure.
Noble rot: a fungus that concentrates sugar and acid in grapes for sweet wines.
The harmful form of Botrytis that ruins grapes in wet conditions.
A tiny louse that destroys vine roots; most vines are grafted onto resistant American rootstock.
The root part of a grafted vine, often American, chosen for pest resistance or vigor.
A fungal disease that thrives in warm, wet weather, attacking leaves and fruit.
A fungal disease that coats green parts of the vine in grey powder, even in dry weather.
The vine's shoots and leaves above ground.
Positioning shoots and leaves to control sunlight on the grapes and airflow.
A cane-pruned training system with one or two canes tied along a wire.
A free-standing, head-trained vine, common in hot, dry regions (gobelet).
Vertical shoot positioning: shoots trained upwards between wires.
The amount of grapes or wine produced per hectare.
The direction a vineyard slope faces.
The difference between daytime and night-time temperatures.
Supplying water to vines artificially; banned or restricted in many European regions.
Older vines (often 35+ years) with lower yields and more concentrated fruit.
Aromas from the grape and alcoholic fermentation: fruit, floral, herbal, spice.
Aromas from winemaking: yeast, malolactic conversion, oak.
Aromas from ageing: leather, earth, honey, nuts, dried fruit.
Compounds that give green pepper and grassy aromas.
The compound behind the petrol note in aged Riesling.
The compound responsible for black pepper aromas in Syrah and Grüner Veltliner.
Sparkling wine whose second fermentation happens in the bottle (méthode champenoise).
Sparkling wine whose second fermentation happens in a pressure tank (Charmat).
The breakdown of dead yeast cells, giving bread, biscuit and brioche notes.
Gradually turning and tilting bottles so sediment collects in the neck (remuage).
Removing the frozen plug of yeast sediment from the bottle neck.
Wine and sugar added after disgorgement to set the sweetness of sparkling wine.
Dry sparkling wine (0–12 g/L of sugar). Brut Nature has almost none.
Confusingly, a sparkling wine slightly sweeter than Brut (12–17 g/L).
White wine from white grapes only; in Champagne, 100% Chardonnay.
White wine made from black grapes.
A blend of several years, made to a consistent house style.
French traditional-method sparkling wine from outside Champagne.
Spanish traditional-method sparkling wine.
Adding grape spirit to wine, during or after fermentation.
A film of yeast that grows on Fino and Manzanilla Sherry, protecting it from oxygen.
A system of fractional blending through tiers of barrels, used for Sherry.
Port aged in small casks, becoming brownish and nutty.
Late Bottled Vintage Port: single-year Port aged 4–6 years in wood before bottling.
Port from a declared exceptional year, bottled young to age for decades.
Botrytized grapes used to make sweet Tokaji in Hungary.
Sweet wine from grapes frozen on the vine.
Italian wine made from dried grapes.
Drying grapes after harvest to concentrate them, as for Amarone.
The lightest German Prädikat level, usually delicate and often off-dry.
German 'late harvest', riper than Kabinett.
German 'selected harvest' of very ripe bunches.
Germany's rarest sweet wine, from individually picked shriveled botrytized berries.
German for dry.
'Great growth': the top vineyard classification in Burgundy, Alsace and Champagne.
'First growth': in Burgundy, the level below Grand Cru; in Bordeaux, the very top estates.
A Bordeaux wine estate, with or without a castle.
A wine estate, especially in Burgundy.
A merchant who buys grapes, juice or wine to blend, bottle and sell under their own label.
A Médoc classification of good estates outside the 1855 list.
Bordeaux's Médoc and Graves, west of the Gironde and Garonne: Cabernet-led.
Bordeaux's Saint-Émilion and Pomerol, east of the Dordogne: Merlot-led.
A Tuscan red made outside traditional rules, often with Cabernet or Merlot.
The historic heartland of an Italian wine area, such as Chianti Classico.
A wine aged longer before release, under Italian or Spanish rules.
Spanish red aged at least two years, including six months to a year in oak.
Spain's longest-aged category: at least five years for red Rioja, two in oak.
Wild Mediterranean herbs (thyme, rosemary, lavender) and the aroma they lend southern French reds.
A loose term for stony, saline or flinty notes, often in high-acid whites.
Sulfur-like aromas (struck match, rubber) from too little oxygen during winemaking.
A spoilage yeast giving barnyard, plaster or sticking-plaster aromas.
Vinegary or nail-varnish aromas from acetic acid and ethyl acetate.
Balance, Length, Intensity, Complexity: the four tests of wine quality.
When fruit, acidity, tannin, alcohol and sweetness are in harmony.
Many different aromas and flavors working together.
An antioxidant and antimicrobial added to almost all wines.
A metal closure that keeps wine fresh and avoids cork taint.
Large egg-shaped clay vessels buried in the ground, used in Georgia since ancient times.
A 1.5-liter bottle: two standard bottles.
A 3-liter bottle (four standard bottles) in Champagne and Burgundy; in Bordeaux traditionally 4.5 liters.
The texture of a wine: silky, creamy, grippy, coarse.
Another word for the finish: how long the flavor lasts.
Streaks running down the glass after swirling; a sign of alcohol and sugar, not quality.
The edge of the wine in a tilted glass, which reveals age.
The center of the wine in the glass, where color intensity is judged.

styles.name: Light, crisp whites
styles.summary: Pale, high in acidity, unoaked and refreshing.
styles.how: Cool climates or early picking keep acidity high and alcohol moderate. Fermented cool in stainless steel and released young.
styles.taste: Citrus, green apple and pear; light body; zesty finish.

styles.name: Aromatic whites
styles.summary: Perfumed grapes that smell of flowers, spice and fruit.
styles.how: Usually unoaked, so the grape's own aromas (terpenes) take center stage.
styles.taste: Rose, lychee, blossom, peach and citrus; dry to off-dry.

styles.name: Full-bodied whites
styles.summary: Rich, round whites, often with oak and malolactic conversion.
styles.how: Riper fruit from warmer sites, fermentation or ageing in oak, lees stirring (bâtonnage) and malolactic conversion add weight and texture.
styles.taste: Ripe stone and tropical fruit, butter, vanilla, toast; creamy texture.

styles.name: Rosé
styles.summary: Pink wines made from black grapes with brief skin contact.
styles.how: Skins soak in the juice for hours rather than days (or are pressed directly), then the juice is fermented cool like a white wine.
styles.taste: Strawberry, raspberry, citrus and melon; usually dry and fresh.

styles.name: Orange wine
styles.summary: White grapes fermented on their skins like a red.
styles.how: Skin contact for days or months gives amber color, texture and some tannin. An ancient method from Georgia, where wines are made in clay qvevri.
styles.taste: Dried apricot, orange peel, tea and nuts; grippy, savory finish.

styles.name: Light reds
styles.summary: Pale, fresh and fruity reds with soft tannins.
styles.how: Thin-skinned grapes, cooler climates and gentle extraction. Often best served lightly chilled.
styles.taste: Red cherry, raspberry, cranberry; high acidity, low tannin.

styles.name: Medium-bodied reds
styles.summary: The versatile middle: food-friendly reds with moderate tannin.
styles.how: Moderate climates and balanced extraction; often some oak.
styles.taste: Red and black fruit, sometimes herbs, spice and earth.

styles.name: Full-bodied reds
styles.summary: Deep, powerful reds with high tannin and alcohol.
styles.how: Thick-skinned grapes, warm sunny climates, long extraction and new oak.
styles.taste: Black fruit, spice, vanilla, chocolate; firm tannins and a long finish.

styles.name: Champagne
styles.summary: The benchmark sparkling wine, made by the traditional method in northern France.
styles.how: Second fermentation in bottle, then at least 15 months on lees (36 for vintage). Mostly Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Meunier.
styles.taste: Citrus, apple, biscuit, brioche and toast; fine persistent bubbles; high acidity.

styles.name: Cava
styles.summary: Spain's traditional-method sparkling wine, mostly from Penedès.
styles.how: Traditional method with native grapes Macabeo, Xarel·lo and Parellada; minimum nine months on lees.
styles.taste: Citrus, apple, almond and a gentle toastiness; great value.

styles.name: Prosecco
styles.summary: Light, fruity Italian fizz from the Glera grape, made in tanks.
styles.how: Tank method: second fermentation in a pressure tank, keeping fresh pear, apple and floral aromas.
styles.taste: Pear, green apple, melon, white flowers; light body; often Extra Dry (slightly sweet).

styles.name: Crémant & other traditional method
styles.summary: French traditional-method sparkling wines from outside Champagne, plus New World versions.
styles.how: Same method as Champagne, usually with shorter lees ageing and local grapes.
styles.taste: Fresh fruit with some bready notes; excellent value.

styles.name: Asti & Moscato d'Asti
styles.summary: Sweet, low-alcohol, grapey sparklers from Piedmont.
styles.how: A single fermentation in a pressure tank, stopped early by chilling so sugar and some bubbles remain (Asti method).
styles.taste: Grapes, peach, orange blossom; sweet, light, about 5–7.5% abv.

styles.name: Noble rot wines
styles.summary: Luscious wines from grapes concentrated by Botrytis cinerea.
styles.how: In misty autumn mornings and sunny afternoons, botrytis pierces the skins; water evaporates and sugar, acid and flavor concentrate. Grapes are picked berry by berry over several passes.
styles.taste: Honey, apricot, marmalade, ginger and saffron; very sweet yet balanced by acidity.

styles.name: Icewine
styles.summary: Pressed from grapes frozen on the vine.
styles.how: Grapes hang into winter and freeze at about −8 °C or below. Pressed while frozen, only a few drops of concentrated sugary juice emerge.
styles.taste: Pure, intense fruit (peach, lychee, citrus) with vivid acidity; no botrytis notes.

styles.name: Dried-grape wines
styles.summary: Grapes dried after harvest to concentrate sugar.
styles.how: Bunches dry on mats, racks or in lofts for weeks or months (appassimento or passito) before pressing.
styles.taste: Raisin, fig, dried cherry, nuts; sweet, or dry and powerful if fully fermented (Amarone).

styles.name: Ruby, Reserve & Vintage Port
styles.summary: Deep, sweet, fruit-driven fortified reds from the Douro.
styles.how: Fortified mid-fermentation, then aged in large vessels or bottle to preserve fruit. Vintage Port spends about two years in wood, then ages for decades in bottle.
styles.taste: Blackberry, black cherry, chocolate, spice; sweet, tannic, about 20% abv.

styles.name: Tawny Port
styles.summary: Port aged in small casks for nutty, oxidative character.
styles.how: Long oxidative ageing in small barrels turns the wine tawny. Indications of age (10, 20, 30, 40 years) are blends showing an average character.
styles.taste: Walnut, toffee, caramel, dried fig and orange peel.

styles.name: Fino & Manzanilla
styles.summary: Bone-dry, pale Sherries aged under a blanket of flor yeast.
styles.how: Fortified to about 15% so flor can grow. The flor protects the wine from oxygen and adds bread dough and almond notes.
styles.taste: Almond, bread dough, chamomile, saline; dry and tangy. Serve chilled.

styles.name: Oloroso & sweet Sherries
styles.summary: Sherries aged in contact with oxygen; dry unless sweetened.
styles.how: Fortified to about 17%, which prevents flor. Oxidative ageing in a solera darkens the wine and builds nutty flavors. Sweet styles use PX or Moscatel, or are blended (Cream).
styles.taste: Walnut, toffee, leather, dried fruit; PX is raisiny and syrupy.

styles.name: Madeira
styles.summary: Heated, oxidized fortified wine from a Portuguese island; nearly indestructible.
styles.how: Fortified, then heated (estufagem in tanks, or canteiro in warm lofts for years). Styles run from dry Sercial to rich Malmsey.
styles.taste: Caramel, toffee, walnut, orange peel; tangy acidity whatever the sweetness.

styles.name: Vins doux naturels
styles.summary: Southern French sweet wines fortified during fermentation.
styles.how: Grape spirit added early, like Port, keeping natural grape sugar. Made from Muscat (fresh, floral) or Grenache (Banyuls, Maury: red, sometimes oxidative).
styles.taste: Muscat: orange blossom, grape, peach. Grenache: red fruit, chocolate, coffee.

steps.title: Sugar
steps.text: Ripe grapes are full of sugar (glucose and fructose).

steps.title: Yeast
steps.text: Yeast, natural or added, feeds on the sugar.

steps.title: Alcohol
steps.text: Sugar becomes **alcohol** and **carbon dioxide**, plus heat and flavor compounds.

steps.title: CO₂
steps.text: Usually escapes. Trap it and you get bubbles.

steps.title: Harvest
steps.text: Grapes picked at the right balance of sugar and acid, often in the cool of morning.

steps.title: Crush & press
steps.text: Juice is separated from skins **before** fermentation, so the wine stays pale.

steps.title: Cool fermentation
steps.text: Usually 12–22 °C in stainless steel to keep fresh fruit aromas.

steps.title: Optional maturation
steps.text: On lees, in oak, or with malolactic conversion for richer styles.

steps.title: Clarify & bottle
steps.text: Fined, filtered, stabilized and bottled.

steps.title: Harvest
steps.text: Black grapes picked when skins and seeds are ripe.

steps.title: Crush
steps.text: Grapes are lightly crushed; juice stays **with the skins**.

steps.title: Warm fermentation
steps.text: 20–32 °C extracts color and tannin. The cap of skins is punched down or pumped over.

steps.title: Maceration
steps.text: Skins may stay in after fermentation to extract more.

steps.title: Press
steps.text: The new wine is drained and the skins pressed.

steps.title: Maturation
steps.text: Malolactic conversion, then months or years in tank or oak before bottling.

steps.title: Black grapes
steps.text: Rosé is made from black grapes.

steps.title: Short skin contact
steps.text: A few hours to a couple of days, just enough for a pink color.

steps.title: Run off or press
steps.text: Juice is separated from the skins, or grapes are pressed directly.

steps.title: Ferment like a white
steps.text: Cool temperatures keep fresh red-fruit aromas.

steps.title: Base wine
steps.text: A high-acid, still, dry wine, often a blend.

steps.title: Liqueur de tirage
steps.text: Wine, sugar and yeast are added and the bottle is sealed with a crown cap.

steps.title: Second fermentation
steps.text: In the bottle. The CO₂ is trapped and dissolves: the wine becomes sparkling.

steps.title: Ageing on lees
steps.text: Months to years in contact with dead yeast: biscuit, bread and brioche aromas (autolysis).

steps.title: Riddling
steps.text: Bottles are turned and tilted until the yeast collects in the neck.

steps.title: Disgorgement
steps.text: The neck is frozen and the plug of yeast shoots out.

steps.title: Dosage
steps.text: A little wine and sugar sets the sweetness, from Brut Nature to Doux.

steps.title: Base wine
steps.text: Often from aromatic grapes such as Glera.

steps.title: Second fermentation in tank
steps.text: In a large sealed pressure tank, not in bottle.

steps.title: Filter & bottle
steps.text: Filtered and bottled under pressure, ready to drink.

steps.title: Result
steps.text: Fresh, fruity and floral, with little or no yeasty character. Prosecco is the best-known example.

steps.title: Whole bunches
steps.text: Uncrushed bunches go into a vessel filled with carbon dioxide.

steps.title: Fermentation inside the berry
steps.text: Without oxygen, an enzyme starts converting sugar to alcohol inside each grape.

steps.title: Press
steps.text: Berries burst or are pressed; fermentation finishes as normal.

steps.title: Result
steps.text: Deep color, soft tannins, and aromas of banana, kirsch and bubblegum: classic Beaujolais Nouveau.

steps.title: Stop the fermentation
steps.text: Chill, filter or add alcohol (fortification) while sugar remains.

steps.title: Late harvest
steps.text: Leave grapes on the vine to ripen and shrivel: Spätlese, Vendanges Tardives.

steps.title: Noble rot
steps.text: *Botrytis cinerea* pierces the skins and concentrates sugar and acid: Sauternes, Tokaji, Beerenauslese.

steps.title: Frozen grapes
steps.text: Grapes freeze on the vine and are pressed frozen, leaving concentrated juice: Icewine, Eiswein.

steps.title: Dried grapes
steps.text: Grapes are dried after picking (passito): Recioto, Vin Santo, Pedro Ximénez.

steps.title: Sweet reserve
steps.text: Unfermented grape juice blended back into dry wine.

steps.title: Douro grapes
steps.text: Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca and other native black grapes.

steps.title: Intense extraction
steps.text: Traditionally foot-trodden in stone lagares; now often robotic treaders.

steps.title: Fortify early
steps.text: Halfway through fermentation, grape spirit (77% abv) is added. Yeast dies and sugar remains.

steps.title: Mature
steps.text: **Ruby** styles in large vessels to keep fruit; **tawny** styles in small casks for oxidative, nutty character.

steps.title: Palomino base wine
steps.text: A neutral, dry white from the chalky albariza soils around Jerez.

steps.title: Fortification
steps.text: To 15–15.5% for biological ageing (fino) or 17% for oxidative ageing (oloroso).

steps.title: Flor or oxygen
steps.text: **Flor**, a layer of yeast, protects Fino and Manzanilla from oxygen. Without flor, Oloroso oxidizes and darkens.

steps.title: Solera
steps.text: Fractional blending across rows of barrels keeps the style consistent year after year.

steps.title: Look
steps.text: Clarity, intensity and color, against a white background.

steps.title: Smell
steps.text: Swirl, then sniff. Intensity first, then the aroma families.

steps.title: Taste
steps.text: Sweetness, acidity, tannin, alcohol, body, flavors and the length of the finish.

steps.title: Conclude
steps.text: Quality and readiness: is it balanced, intense, complex and long?

steps.title: New barrels
steps.text: Add flavor: vanilla, toast, clove, coconut, smoke.

steps.title: Slow oxygen
steps.text: Tiny amounts of oxygen through the staves soften tannin and deepen color.

steps.title: Old barrels
steps.text: Add little flavor but still allow gentle oxygen exposure.

steps.title: Cheaper options
steps.text: Oak chips or staves in a tank add oak flavors quickly, without the oxygen effect.

items.name: Clarity
items.tip: Most wines are clear. Haze can mean a fault, or an unfiltered natural wine.

items.name: Intensity
items.tip: Look down through the glass at the core. Can you see the stem through a red?

items.name: Color
items.tip: For whites. Reds run **purple → ruby → garnet → tawny → brown**; rosés are **pink, salmon, orange**.

items.name: Condition
items.tip: Musty, wet-cardboard notes suggest cork taint (TCA). Flat bruised-apple notes suggest oxidation.

items.name: Intensity
items.tip: Do the aromas leap out, or do you have to search for them?

items.name: Development
items.tip: Only fresh fruit means youthful. Tertiary notes (leather, honey, nuts) mean it is developing.

items.name: Characteristics
items.tip: Work through the aroma families: fruit, floral, herbal, spice, then winemaking and ageing notes.

items.name: Sweetness
items.tip: Feel it on the tip of the tongue. Ripe fruit flavors can feel sweet in a dry wine, so be careful.

items.name: Acidity
items.tip: How much does your mouth water? How sharp is it on the sides of the tongue?

items.name: Tannin
items.tip: The drying, gripping feeling on gums and teeth. Note its texture too: fine, ripe, coarse or green.

items.name: Alcohol
items.tip: A warming feeling at the back of the throat. Below 11% is low; 14% and above is high.

items.name: Body
items.tip: The weight of the wine in your mouth: think skimmed milk versus whole milk versus cream.

items.name: Finish
items.tip: How long do pleasant flavors linger after swallowing or spitting?

items.name: Quality
items.tip: Use **BLIC**: Balance, Length, Intensity and Complexity. The more boxes ticked, the higher the quality.

items.name: Readiness
items.tip: Does it have the fruit, acid and tannin to improve? Or is it at its peak now?

pairings.effect: Sweet food makes wine taste **drier, more acidic, more bitter** and less fruity.
pairings.tip: Pick a wine at least as sweet as the dish: Sauternes with crème brûlée, Moscato d'Asti with fruit tarts.

pairings.effect: Umami (mushrooms, cured meat, aged cheese, soy) makes wine taste **more bitter, more acidic** and less sweet and fruity.
pairings.tip: Choose fruity, low-tannin wines, or add salt or acid to the dish.

pairings.effect: Acidic food makes wine taste **less acidic**, and fruitier and sweeter.
pairings.tip: Match high-acid dishes with high-acid wines: goat cheese with Sancerre, tomato pasta with Chianti.

pairings.effect: Salty food makes wine taste **less bitter and less acidic**, and fuller.
pairings.tip: A friendly partner: oysters with Muscadet or Chablis, salty cheese with Port.

pairings.effect: Chili makes wine taste **more bitter, more alcoholic and more acidic**, and increases the burning sensation.
pairings.tip: Choose off-dry, low-alcohol, low-tannin whites: Riesling Kabinett, Gewürztraminer.

pairings.effect: Fat and protein **soften tannin** and coat the palate.
pairings.tip: Steak with Cabernet Sauvignon or Barolo: the meat tames the wine's grip.

pairings.effect: Bitter food (radicchio, dark chocolate, grilled char) adds to the **bitterness** of tannic wines.
pairings.tip: Choose low-tannin wines with ripe fruit.

pairings.effect: Delicate dishes are overwhelmed by powerful wines, and vice versa.
pairings.tip: Match light with light (sole and Pinot Grigio) and rich with rich (lamb tagine and Châteauneuf-du-Pape).

pairings.effect: Food and wine that grew up together usually work together.
pairings.tip: Bistecca with Chianti, choucroute with Alsace Riesling, Sherry with jamón and tapas.

labels.title: Bordeaux
labels.summary: Bordeaux labels lead with the château, then the appellation. Classified growths say so.

fields.note: The estate's flagship wine (as opposed to a second wine).
**Producer.** A château is an estate with its own vineyards, castle or not.
**Classification.** One of the 61 Médoc estates ranked in 1855 (First to Fifth Growth).
**Appellation.** The more specific the place, the higher the expectations: Bordeaux → Haut-Médoc → Margaux.
Confirms the AOC (PDO). No grape names: it's a blend, mostly Cabernet Sauvignon here.
**Vintage.** Weather varies a lot in Bordeaux, so the year matters.
**Estate bottled.** Made and bottled at the property.

labels.title: Burgundy
labels.summary: In Burgundy the vineyard is king. The quality level is shown by how specific the place name is.

fields.note: **Village.** A village-level wine names the commune.
**Premier Cru + climat.** The named vineyard is a Premier Cru. A Grand Cru would show only the vineyard name, e.g. *Chambertin*.
No grape on the label: red Burgundy is Pinot Noir, white is Chardonnay.
**Vintage.**
**Producer.** *Domaine* = grower-producer. *Maison* usually means a négociant who buys grapes.

labels.title: Champagne
labels.summary: Champagne labels show the house, the style, the sweetness and a small code revealing who made it.

fields.note: **House.** Most Champagne is sold by brand.
Only sparkling wine from the Champagne region may use this word.
**Style.** Blanc de Blancs = Chardonnay only. Grand Cru = grapes from top-rated villages.
**Sweetness.** Brut Nature < Extra Brut < Brut < Extra Dry < Sec < Demi-Sec < Doux.
No year: a blend of several harvests for consistency. A vintage Champagne shows one year.
**Maker code.** NM = house buying grapes; RM = grower making their own; CM = co-operative.

labels.title: Alsace
labels.summary: Unusually for France, Alsace names the grape. Look for Grand Cru and late-harvest terms.

fields.note: **Producer.**
**Grape variety.** Alsace labels are varietal.
**Grand Cru** + vineyard name: one of 51 top sites.
**Late harvest**, usually sweet. *Sélection de Grains Nobles* = botrytized.
**Vintage.**
Tall flûte bottle is required.

labels.title: Rhône
labels.summary: Rhône labels name the appellation; the papal crossed keys mark many Châteauneuf-du-Pape bottles.

fields.note: **Producer.**
**Appellation.** A cru of the Southern Rhône: Grenache-led blends of up to 13 varieties.
'Old vines': no legal definition, but signals lower yields.
**Vintage.**

fields.text: Mis en bouteille à la propriété
fields.note: Estate bottled.

labels.title: Germany
labels.summary: German labels pack in region, village + vineyard, grape and a ripeness level (Prädikat).

fields.note: **Producer.** Weingut = wine estate.
**Region** (Anbaugebiet).
**Village + vineyard.** Wehlen (village, with -er) and Sonnenuhr (the 'sundial' vineyard).
**Grape + Prädikat.** Spätlese = late harvest ripeness; often lusciously off-dry unless *trocken*.
**Dry.** Halbtrocken/feinherb = off-dry.
**Vintage.**
Quality category and official control number.

labels.title: Italy
labels.summary: Italian labels name the place (sometimes the grape), the category (DOCG) and ageing terms.

fields.note: **Producer.** Fattoria, Tenuta, Castello = estate.
**Denomination.** The historic heart of Chianti: mostly Sangiovese.
**Top tier**: estate fruit, longest ageing. Below it: Riserva, then annata.
Denominazione di Origine Controllata e Garantita: Italy's highest category.
**Vintage.**
Estate bottled. The black rooster neck seal marks Chianti Classico.

labels.title: Spain
labels.summary: Spanish labels show the region and an ageing category that tells you how long it rested.

fields.note: **Producer.** Bodega = winery.
**Region** (DOCa). Mostly Tempranillo.
**Ageing.** Joven → Crianza (2 yrs) → Reserva (3) → Gran Reserva (5, at least 2 in oak).
Spain's top category (DOCa / DOQ).
**Cosecha** = vintage.

labels.title: Port
labels.summary: Port labels name the shipper and the style; the style tells you how it was aged.

fields.note: **Shipper / quinta.** A quinta is a Douro estate.
**Style.** Declared only in great years, bottled after ~2 years, ages for decades. Needs decanting.
(Alternative) LBV: single year, 4–6 years in wood, ready to drink.
(Alternative) An *indication of age*: a tawny blend tasting of about 20 years.
**Vintage** (only on vintage, LBV and Colheita styles).
Fortified: about 19–22% abv.

labels.title: USA
labels.summary: New World labels lead with the brand and the grape; the AVA tells you where.

fields.note: **Brand / winery.**
**Grape.** At least 75% of the named variety (US rule).
**AVA.** At least 85% of grapes from the named AVA.
No legal meaning in the US: the producer's own top tier.
**Vintage.** At least 95% from that year when an AVA is named.
Estate = grown on land the winery owns or controls.

labels.title: Australia
labels.summary: Australian labels show brand, grape and the GI (Geographical Indication).

fields.note: **Brand.**
**Grape** (85% rule). 'Old vine' is defined by the Barossa Old Vine Charter: 35+ years.
**GI** (region).
**Vintage.**
Most Australian wines use screwcaps.
